summary: A nearly blind river dolphin that navigates the silt-thick Indus entirely by echolocation, swimming on its side and trailing a flipper along the riverbed. Once spread through the whole Indus system, it is now trapped between irrigation barrages in a few stretches of the Indus in Pakistan, with a tiny remnant in India's Beas River. It was recognised as a separate species from the Ganges dolphin in 2021.
nativeRange: Indus River, Pakistan (mainly between Chashma and Kotri barrages); a remnant population in the Beas River, Punjab, India
abilities: Its eyes have no crystalline lens; it can probably sense only light and its direction, and relies on near-continuous echolocation clicks
Swims on its side, sweeping its head and a pectoral flipper across the bottom to find prey in near-zero visibility
Long, narrow beak with interlocking needle teeth that remain visible when the mouth is closed
Unfused neck vertebrae let it turn its head sharply, unlike most dolphins

animal.diet: Fish and freshwater prawns, taken from the riverbed and mid-water
animal.habitat: Deep channels, confluences and eddies of the turbid main Indus; needs water depth through the dry season
animal.size: About 1.5–2.5 m long; females larger than males; roughly 70–110 kg
animal.behaviour: Surfaces every minute or two with a brief, low roll and a sneeze-like blow, then vanishes; it rarely leaps or bow-rides. Usually seen singly or in loose groups at channel junctions.
fieldMarks: Silhouette at the surface: a brief low arc showing a long, thin beak, rounded melon and only a low triangular hump instead of a true dorsal fin
Grey-brown body, often pinkish on the belly; broad, paddle-like flippers
Blow is a short, audible puff with little visible spray
Usually seen in muddy main channels below or between barrages, often near confluences
animal.lookalikes: The Ganges river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) looks almost identical but lives in the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna and Karnaphuli systems; range alone separates them. No other dolphin occurs in the Indus.
animal.whereToSee: Indus Dolphin Reserve between Guddu and Sukkur barrages, Sindh, Pakistan; the Taunsa Barrage Wildlife Sanctuary, Punjab; Beas Conservation Reserve near Harike, Punjab, India
animal.season: Resident year-round; easiest to see in the low-water months of winter and early spring, when dolphins concentrate in deeper channels

lore: In Sindhi folklore the bhulan was once a woman, turned into a blind dolphin after she was cursed by a holy man. Since 1992 the Sindh Wildlife Department and WWF-Pakistan have run a programme rescuing dolphins stranded in irrigation canals.
funFact: Surveys counted around 1,800–2,000 Indus dolphins in recent years, almost all in a stretch of river shorter than 1,000 km.

summary: A great wild goat of the western Himalaya, Hindu Kush and Karakoram, whose males carry immense corkscrew horns and a flowing ruff. It is Pakistan's national animal and a conservation success story: community-run trophy-hunting programmes helped populations recover enough for the species to move from Endangered to Near Threatened in 2015.
nativeRange: Northern Pakistan, eastern Afghanistan, Kashmir (India), southern Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan
abilities: Climbs near-vertical cliffs and even into holm-oak trees to browse
Males' spiralling horns can exceed 1.5 m along the curve
Feeds at high altitude in summer and descends to lower slopes in winter, tracking snowline

animal.diet: Grasses and herbs in spring and summer; browses leaves and twigs of oak, juniper and shrubs in winter
animal.habitat: Steep, rugged terrain with scrub or open woodland, roughly 600–3,600 m
animal.size: Shoulder height 65–115 cm; males up to about 110 kg, females much smaller
animal.behaviour: Males live apart from females and young for most of the year and join them for the winter rut, when they clash horns and rear up in contests on steep ground.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: stocky goat with outward-twisting corkscrew horns (males) — the spiral, not a backward arc, is diagnostic
Adult males have a long ruff of shaggy hair on the throat, chest and shins
Coat greyish-tan, paler in winter; females are reddish, short-horned and lack the ruff
Signs: goat-type pellet piles on ledges and cloven, blunt-tipped hoofprints on cliff paths
animal.lookalikes: Siberian ibex has long, scimitar-shaped horns sweeping back with knobbly ridges, not corkscrews. Urial (wild sheep) have curling horns that circle beside the face and lack a goat beard.
animal.whereToSee: Chitral Gol National Park and Tooshi-Shasha Conservancy, Chitral; Kargah and Gilgit-Baltistan community conservancies; Torghar Hills, Balochistan; Kazinag National Park, Kashmir
animal.season: Resident; males are easiest to see near villages and lower slopes during the winter rut (November–January)

lore: The name is popularly read as Persian 'snake-eater', and in Hindu Kush folklore markhor were said to kill snakes and leave a foam whose dried residue was used to draw out snake venom. The Torghar Conservation Project, begun by Pashtun tribesmen in 1985, is a celebrated model of community-led wildlife recovery.
funFact: A Pakistani markhor trophy-hunting permit has sold for more than US$100,000, with most of the fee going to the local community.

summary: The only truly social cat, living in prides of related females with one or a few resident males. Lions once ranged from southern Europe and the Middle East to India and across Africa; today they survive in sub-Saharan Africa and one small Asian outpost, the Gir forest and surrounding lands of Gujarat, India. Asiatic lions (Panthera leo leo, in the current northern subspecies) grew from a few dozen around 1900 to 891 counted in Gujarat's 2025 census.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa; in Asia only the Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat, India (Gir National Park and surrounding districts)
abilities: Cooperative hunters: lionesses fan out and ambush to bring down buffalo, zebra and even young elephants
Roar audible to people up to about 8 km away, used to advertise territory
Can eat over 30 kg of meat in a single sitting, then rest for most of a day
As apex predators they shape the behaviour and numbers of large grazers

animal.diet: Carnivore: wildebeest, zebra, buffalo, antelope in Africa; in Gir mainly chital, sambar, nilgai, wild boar and livestock
animal.habitat: Open savanna, grassland, dry woodland and scrub with water; in Gir, dry teak forest, scrub and farmland
animal.lifespan: Females about 15–18 years, males often 10–12 in the wild
animal.size: Males 150–250 kg, about 2.5–3.3 m including tail; females 110–180 kg
animal.behaviour: Prides defend territories for generations; incoming males often kill young cubs to bring females back into breeding. In Gir, prides are smaller and males and females usually associate only to mate or share large kills.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: large, plain tawny cat with a tufted black tail-tip — the only cat with a tail tuft
Adult males with a mane; Asiatic males' manes are usually shorter, showing the ears
Asiatic lions typically have a longitudinal fold of skin along the belly, rare in African lions
Tracks: round prints about 11–14 cm across, four toes, no claw marks, a three-lobed rear edge to the heel pad
animal.voice: A deep, rolling series of moaning roars that fade into grunts, given most at dusk and before dawn, often by several pride members together.
animal.lookalikes: Female lions can be confused with pumas in zoos or photos, but the two never overlap in the wild; lionesses are much larger and have the tail tuft. Leopards are spotted with rosettes.
animal.whereToSee: Gir National Park and Devalia Safari Park, Gujarat; Serengeti and Ngorongoro (Tanzania); Maasai Mara (Kenya); Okavango Delta (Botswana); Kruger (South Africa)
animal.season: Resident year-round; Gir is closed to safaris 16 June–15 October for the monsoon, and dry seasons give the best sightings in Africa

lore: The lion capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, four lions back to back, is the national emblem of India. The Nawab of Junagadh protected Gir's last lions in the early 1900s, saving the Asian population from extinction.
funFact: In 2025 about 57% of Gujarat's lions were counted outside Gir's protected core, living among farms and coastal villages.

summary: A single-horned rhino with skin folded like riveted armour plates, living in the tall floodplain grasslands of the Brahmaputra and the Nepal terai. From fewer than 200 animals in the early 1900s it has recovered to over 4,000, one of Asia's great conservation comebacks, about two-thirds of them in Kaziranga National Park.
nativeRange: Northeast India (Assam, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh) and lowland Nepal; formerly across the Indus and Ganges plains
abilities: Grazes tall elephant grass, keeping floodplain grasslands open for other species
Strong swimmer that crosses rivers and wallows for hours
Defends itself mainly with sharp lower tusks (incisors) rather than its horn
Uses communal dung heaps (middens) that act as scent noticeboards

animal.diet: Grasses, reeds, aquatic plants, fruit, leaves and crops
animal.habitat: Alluvial floodplain grassland, swamps and adjoining forest
animal.size: 1.7–2 m at shoulder; males about 2,000–2,700 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary, but gathers at wallows and grazing lawns. Feeds mainly in the morning and evening and lies in mud or water through the heat of the day.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: massive grey body with deep skin folds at shoulder, flank and rump giving an 'armour-plated' look
Single horn, usually 20–30 cm, on the nose
Skin covered with wart-like bumps on the shoulders and legs
Signs: large dung middens along trails, three-toed tracks about 25 cm across, wallows in mud
animal.lookalikes: The Javan rhino (also one-horned) survives only in Ujung Kulon, Java, and has finer, mosaic-like skin texture without warts. The African white and black rhinos have two horns.
animal.whereToSee: Kaziranga, Pobitora and Manas national parks (Assam); Jaldapara and Gorumara (West Bengal); Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh); Chitwan and Bardia (Nepal)
animal.season: Resident; Kaziranga is open roughly November–April, closed through the monsoon floods

lore: Rhinos appear on several Indus Valley Civilisation seals from Mohenjo-daro, and the Mughal emperor Babur recorded hunting them near Peshawar in the early 1500s. Albrecht Dürer's famous 1515 woodcut depicts an Indian rhino sent from Gujarat to Lisbon.
funFact: Dürer never saw the animal he drew: his armour-plated rhino, based on a sketch and a letter, remained Europe's standard image of a rhino into the 18th century.

summary: A small, slender fox of open plains, found only on the Indian subcontinent. It favours short grassland and semi-desert, avoiding dense forest, and hunts insects and rodents mostly at dusk and night.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh, from the Himalayan foothills to Tamil Nadu
abilities: Digs complex dens with several entrances, reused over many years
Eats large numbers of rodents, termites and crop pests
Pairs bond and both parents provision the pups

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects, rodents, reptiles, birds' eggs and fruits such as ber and neem
animal.habitat: Open short grassland, scrub and semi-desert; avoids dense forest and steep terrain
animal.size: Body 45–60 cm plus a 25–35 cm tail; 2–4 kg
animal.behaviour: Rests in dens through the heat of day and is most active at dusk and early morning; pups are born in the dry season, around February–March.
fieldMarks: Small, long-legged grey fox with rufous legs
Bushy tail with a distinct black tip
Dark smudge on the muzzle in front of the eyes; ears dark-backed
Signs: dens with several entrances on low mounds in open ground, with scats full of insect parts and seeds
animal.lookalikes: Red fox (desert subspecies in the Thar and Pakistan) is larger, redder above and has a white tail tip. Golden jackal is larger, heavier, and has a less bushy tail without a black tip.
animal.whereToSee: Velavadar Blackbuck National Park and Little Rann of Kutch (Gujarat); Tal Chhapar and Desert National Park (Rajasthan); Rollapadu (Andhra Pradesh); Deccan grasslands around Pune and Bengaluru
animal.season: Resident; pups visible at dens around March–May

lore: Foxes and jackals play the cunning roles in the Panchatantra and Jataka tales. The species was described by George Shaw in 1800, hence the name, though it is now rare there.
funFact: Despite its name, the Bengal fox is now scarce in Bengal itself; its strongholds are the dry grasslands of western and peninsular India.

summary: One of the fastest land mammals, a slim antelope of the Indian plains whose mature males are glossy black and white with long spiralled horns. Once among the most numerous large mammals of South Asia, it survives in protected grasslands and among communities such as the Bishnoi who refuse to harm it.
nativeRange: India and Nepal; extinct in the wild in Bangladesh and Pakistan (reintroduced to Lal Suhanra, Pakistan); introduced in Texas and Argentina
abilities: Can run at up to about 80 km/h and sustain high speeds over long distances
Leaps high in the air while fleeing ('stotting' or pronking)
Males defend small mating territories (leks) in some populations

animal.diet: Grasses; also pods, flowers and crops
animal.habitat: Open short grassland and plains with little tree cover
animal.size: Shoulder height 74–84 cm; 20–57 kg; horns of males up to about 70 cm
animal.behaviour: Lives in herds of females and young with territorial males. Dominant males hold their heads up and back, horns laid along the neck, in displays to rivals.
fieldMarks: Mature males: dark brown to black upperparts sharply divided from white belly; white eye-ring and chin
Corkscrew horns with 3–5 spiral turns (males only)
Females and young males: tan-yellow above, white below, hornless
Signs: territorial males leave large dung middens on their patch
animal.lookalikes: Chinkara (Indian gazelle) is sandy, both sexes have short, near-straight ridged horns, and it has a dark side-stripe. Nilgai is far larger and grey.
animal.whereToSee: Velavadar Blackbuck National Park (Gujarat); Tal Chhapar Sanctuary and Bishnoi villages around Jodhpur (Rajasthan); Point Calimere (Tamil Nadu); Ranibennur (Karnataka); Lal Suhanra National Park (Pakistan)
animal.season: Resident; displays peak in the rut (roughly March–April and August–October, varying by region)

lore: In Hindu tradition the blackbuck is the mount of Chandra, the moon, and Vayu, and its skin was prescribed in Vedic texts for ritual seats. Its hunting by a Bollywood actor near a Bishnoi village in 1998 led to a celebrated conviction.
funFact: The blackbuck is the only living member of the genus Antilope, the genus that gives the antelope subfamily Antilopinae its name.

summary: The largest antelope in Asia, a sloping-backed, horse-like animal of dry plains and farmland in northern and central India. Because many Hindus associate it with the cow, it is widely tolerated, and it has become abundant enough to be a notorious crop raider.
nativeRange: India, eastern Pakistan and southern Nepal; extinct in Bangladesh; introduced in Texas, USA
abilities: Can go long periods without drinking, getting moisture from plants
Thrives alongside agriculture, feeding on crops at night
Males spar on their knees, pushing neck-to-neck

animal.diet: Grasses, herbs, leaves, fruits and pods (e.g. of Prosopis and Acacia) and crops
animal.habitat: Open scrub, dry forest and agricultural land; avoids dense forest
animal.size: 1–1.5 m at shoulder; males up to about 280 kg
animal.behaviour: Herds use shared dung heaps, sometimes dozens of piles at a site, which mark ranges. Females and calves form small herds while bulls live alone or in bachelor groups.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: horse-like, with high shoulders sloping down to lower hindquarters
Adult bulls blue-grey with a white throat patch and a tuft of black hair (a 'beard') on the throat
Females and young tawny-brown; white spots on cheeks and white rings above the hooves
Bulls have short, straight conical horns (about 20 cm); signs include large communal dung middens
animal.lookalikes: Sambar deer is darker, has branched antlers (stags) and a bushy tail, and lives in forest. Gaur is a much heavier, black bovine with curved horns and white 'socks'.
animal.whereToSee: Ranthambore, Keoladeo (Bharatpur) and Tal Chhapar (Rajasthan); Gir and Little Rann of Kutch (Gujarat); farmland across Haryana and Uttar Pradesh
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Mughal emperor Jahangir recorded hunting nilgai in his memoir, the Jahangirnama, and his court painter Ustad Mansur painted the animal from life. Its association with the sacred cow has long protected it, though India's environment ministry declared it vermin in Bihar in December 2015 to allow culling.
funFact: The nilgai is the only living species in its genus, and with the four-horned antelope it forms a tribe (Boselaphini) whose relatives once roamed Europe.

summary: A shaggy, termite-eating bear of India and Sri Lanka that vacuums insects out of their mounds. It lacks upper front incisors, can close its nostrils, and uses its protrusible lips like a suction tube. Despite its insect diet it is one of the most dangerous animals in India, attacking when surprised at close range.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan; possibly extinct in Bangladesh
abilities: Sucks termites from mounds with a whooshing noise audible 100 m away
Long, curved claws dig out termite mounds and bee nests
Mothers carry cubs on their backs for months, a habit not regularly seen in other bears

animal.diet: Termites, ants and other insects; fruit such as mahua flowers, ber and figs; honey
animal.habitat: Dry and moist forest, scrub and rocky hills with boulder caves, generally below 1,500 m
animal.lifespan: About 20 years in the wild; up to 40 in captivity
animal.size: Males 80–145 kg, females 55–95 kg; about 1.5–1.9 m long
animal.behaviour: Largely nocturnal where disturbed. Does not hibernate. Charges when startled, a defensive reaction that accounts for many human injuries.
fieldMarks: Shaggy, unkempt black coat, longest on the shoulders and neck
Pale, mobile muzzle with a long lower lip
White or yellowish U- or Y-shaped chest mark
Signs: termite mounds torn open with scattered soil; tracks show long claw marks well ahead of the toes; scats packed with termite remains
animal.lookalikes: Asiatic black bear has a neat short coat, a V-shaped crescent on the chest, round ears and lives mainly in the Himalaya and northeast. Wild boar from a distance is smaller-headed with a bristly crest.
animal.whereToSee: Daroji Bear Sanctuary (Karnataka); Satpura, Kanha and Tadoba (central India); Ranthambore (Rajasthan); Yala and Wilpattu (Sri Lanka)
animal.season: Resident; mahua flowering (March–April) draws bears into the open

lore: For centuries the Kalandar community trained sloth bears as 'dancing bears'; through a rehabilitation programme led by Wildlife SOS and partners, the practice ended in India around 2009. Kipling's Baloo in The Jungle Book is a sloth bear.
funFact: European naturalists first classified it as a kind of sloth, naming it Bradypus ursinus in 1791 on the strength of its long curved claws and missing upper incisors; the name 'sloth bear' stuck.

summary: The most widespread bear, from Spain and Scandinavia across Siberia to Alaska and the Rockies, including the grizzly and the giant Kodiak bear. In South Asia it survives as the pale, rare Himalayan brown bear (U. a. isabellinus) of Deosai, Ladakh and the Karakoram, a lineage genetically distinct from other brown bears.
nativeRange: Northern Eurasia and northwestern North America; isolated populations in the Pyrenees, Apennines, Carpathians, Caucasus, Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush
abilities: Hibernates for up to 7 months without eating, drinking or urinating
Can smell carcasses from several kilometres away
Salmon-eating bears carry marine nitrogen into forests when they drag fish inland

animal.diet: Omnivore: grasses, roots, berries, nuts, insects, salmon, rodents and large mammals; Himalayan bears dig marmots and graze alpine plants
animal.habitat: Forest, tundra, alpine meadows and high plateaus
animal.size: Highly variable: about 80–600 kg; coastal Alaskan and Kodiak males are largest
animal.behaviour: Solitary except mothers with cubs and gatherings at food sources such as salmon falls. Excavates its own winter den on slopes.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: prominent shoulder hump (digging muscle) and a dished face in profile
Coat ranges from near-black to blond; Himalayan bears are sandy-reddish or pale
Short, round ears
Tracks: hind print up to ~30 cm with long claw marks 5 cm or more ahead of toes, toes in a fairly straight row; signs include dug-out marmot burrows and overturned rocks
animal.lookalikes: American black bear and Asiatic black bear lack the shoulder hump, have a straighter face profile, larger ears and short curved claws. In the Himalaya, the Asiatic black bear has a white chest crescent.
animal.whereToSee: Deosai National Park (Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan); Katmai and Denali (Alaska); Yellowstone (USA); Kamchatka (Russia); Shiretoko (Hokkaido); Cantabrian Mountains (Spain); Finnish–Russian border hides
animal.season: Active roughly April–November; best viewed at salmon runs (July–September) and on Deosai in July–August

lore: The Ainu of Hokkaido held the iyomante ceremony to send a bear's spirit back to the gods. The Greek name Arktos for the bear gave us 'Arctic', the land beneath the Great Bear constellation.
funFact: Deosai National Park was created in 1993 largely to protect Pakistan's Himalayan brown bears, which numbered only around 20 there at the time.

summary: The most widely distributed wild carnivore on Earth, from the Arctic to the deserts of Pakistan and the suburbs of London. Its South Asian forms include the pale desert fox of the Thar and Balochistan and the thick-furred Himalayan red fox. Introduced in Australia, it has helped drive many small marsupials to extinction.
nativeRange: Across the Northern Hemisphere (Europe, Asia including northern South Asia, North Africa, North America); introduced to Australia
abilities: Hears rodents moving beneath snow and dives on them in a high arcing pounce
Caches surplus food and relocates it later by memory and smell
Adapts to cities, raising cubs under sheds and in railway embankments

animal.diet: Omnivore: rodents, rabbits, birds, insects, earthworms, fruit and scavenged food
animal.habitat: Almost any habitat with cover, from tundra to desert to city centres
animal.lifespan: Usually 2–4 years in the wild; up to about 14
animal.size: Body 45–90 cm, tail 30–55 cm; 3–14 kg; desert forms smallest
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal and crepuscular. Pairs share a territory and may be helped by non-breeding young from previous litters.
fieldMarks: Rusty-orange coat with white throat and black-backed ears
Black 'stockings' on the lower legs
Long, bushy tail usually with a white tip
Tracks: neat oval prints about 5 cm long in a near-straight line; strong musky scent at scent posts and dens
animal.voice: Vixens give an eerie, drawn-out scream in winter; both sexes use a sharp triple bark, 'wow-wow-wow'.
animal.lookalikes: Bengal fox is smaller and greyer with a black (not white) tail tip. Golden jackal is larger, greyer, with a shorter tail and longer legs. Arctic fox is smaller-eared and white or blue-grey.
animal.whereToSee: Cities such as London and Bristol; Deosai and Khunjerab (Pakistan) and Ladakh for Himalayan foxes; Desert National Park and the Rann of Kutch for desert foxes; Hokkaido (Japan)
animal.season: Resident; cubs at dens April–June; vixen screams in mating season, December–February

lore: In Japan the kitsune is the messenger of the rice deity Inari, and fox statues guard thousands of Inari shrines. The medieval European beast-epic of Reynard the Fox satirised courts and clergy.
funFact: The Soviet geneticist Dmitry Belyaev bred tame foxes from 1959; within decades they wagged tails, had floppy ears and piebald coats.

summary: The famous snake-fighting mongoose of South Asia, a grizzled grey hunter of gardens, scrub and fields. Speed, a thick coat and modified acetylcholine receptors that resist cobra neurotoxins let it tackle venomous snakes, though most of its diet is rodents, insects and lizards.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, west through Afghanistan and Iran to the Arabian Gulf
abilities: Partially resistant to snake neurotoxins, owing to altered receptor proteins
Moves so fast it can dodge a striking cobra, then bites the back of the head
Hunts by darting in and out of reach, often seizing prey such as rats and lizards with a single bite to the head

animal.diet: Rodents, insects, snakes, lizards, birds, eggs, carrion and fruit
animal.habitat: Open forest, scrub, cultivated land and edges of villages and towns
animal.lifespan: About 7–8 years in the wild; to 12 in captivity
animal.size: Body 36–45 cm, tail 45 cm; about 0.9–1.7 kg
animal.behaviour: Diurnal, unlike many mongooses; usually alone or in pairs. Fluffs its fur to look larger when facing a snake.
fieldMarks: Low, long-bodied grey animal with a grizzled, salt-and-pepper coat
Tail as long as the body, tapering, with a pale or reddish tip
Reddish legs and face around the eyes
Runs with tail held out or slightly raised; tracks show five toes with claws
animal.lookalikes: Small Indian mongoose (Urva auropunctata) is smaller with golden-flecked fur; ruddy mongoose (Urva smithii) has a black tail tip; stripe-necked mongoose has a black neck stripe. Squirrels have bushy tails and climb.
animal.whereToSee: Common in gardens, farmland and parks across India and Pakistan; Sariska and Ranthambore (Rajasthan); Gir (Gujarat); Margalla Hills (Islamabad)
animal.season: Resident; active in daylight year-round

lore: Kubera, Hindu god of wealth, and the Buddhist Jambhala are depicted holding a mongoose that spits jewels. The Panchatantra tells of a loyal mongoose killed by a Brahmin who mistook the blood of a slain snake for that of his baby; Kipling's Rikki-Tikki-Tavi is usually taken to be this species.
funFact: The English word 'mongoose' comes from Marathi/Telugu names such as mangūs and mungisa.

summary: A medium-sized wild dog of South Asia, the Middle East and southeastern Europe, known for its wailing dusk chorus. It is spreading rapidly across Europe, now reaching the Baltic states and beyond. Since 2015 the African populations once called golden jackals are treated as a separate species, the African golden wolf.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia, Middle East, Caucasus, Central Asia and southeastern Europe, expanding north and west
abilities: Scavenges and hunts, cleaning up carcasses and refuse around villages
Coordinates in pairs to hunt rodents, hares and young deer
Expanding its range rapidly as wolves decline and farmland spreads

animal.diet: Omnivore: rodents, hares, birds, fish, insects, carrion, fruit (ber, figs) and human food waste
animal.habitat: Dry open country, scrub, farmland, wetlands and forest edges, often near settlements
animal.size: Body 70–85 cm, tail 20–30 cm; 7–15 kg
animal.behaviour: Mated pairs are long-lasting and defend a territory; older pups may stay to help raise the next litter.
fieldMarks: Medium dog shape, golden to tawny-grey coat with darker saddle
Bushy tail with a black tip, held low
Pale throat; narrow muzzle and pointed ears
Tracks: dog-like, about 5–6 cm, with the two middle toes' pads often fused at the rear
animal.voice: A rising chorus of wails and yips at dusk and night, often set off by sirens; one call starts others across a village.
animal.lookalikes: Indian wolf is larger, longer-legged and greyer. Red fox is smaller with a white tail tip and black-backed ears. Feral dogs vary in colour and lack the black tail tip.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo (Bharatpur) and Ranthambore (Rajasthan); Velavadar (Gujarat); Sundarbans; outskirts of Lahore, Karachi and Delhi; Danube Delta (Romania)
animal.season: Resident; most vocal in winter

lore: The two jackals Karataka and Damanaka narrate the first book of the Panchatantra; its Arabic translation is titled Kalila wa-Dimna after them. In Hindu iconography jackals accompany the goddess Chamunda.
funFact: The word 'jackal' comes via Turkish from Persian shaghāl, ultimately from Sanskrit śṛgāla.

summary: An armour-plated ant- and termite-eater of the Indian subcontinent, covered in overlapping keratin scales and able to roll into a near-impregnable ball. It is one of the most trafficked mammals in the world, poached for its scales and meat, and is protected under Schedule I of India's Wildlife Protection Act.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and possibly Bangladesh
abilities: Toothless; a sticky tongue about 40 cm long, extending some 25 cm from the mouth, reaches deep into termite galleries
Rolls into a tight ball, protected by sharp-edged scales, when threatened
Digs burrows several metres long with powerful foreclaws
Can close its nostrils and ears against biting ants

animal.diet: Ants and termites, including their eggs and larvae
animal.habitat: Grassland, dry and moist forest, scrub and farmland, including hilly and semi-desert terrain
animal.lifespan: Poorly known; up to about 19 years in captivity
animal.size: Head and body 45–75 cm, tail 33–47 cm; about 9–16 kg
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal and solitary, sleeping by day in burrows or rock crevices. Walks on its knuckles and hind feet, sometimes rearing up on its back legs.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: low, tapering body like a walking pine cone, with a broad, thick tail
11–13 rows of large, overlapping yellowish-brown scales on the body
Tiny conical head with small eyes and no visible teeth
Signs: burrows with fresh soil at the entrance, dug-open termite mounds and ant nests, a tail-drag line between footprints
animal.lookalikes: Chinese pangolin (in the northeast Himalayan foothills) has smaller scales, prominent external ears and a shorter tail. Sunda pangolin occurs only in Southeast Asia. No other South Asian mammal has scales.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen; nocturnal surveys in Kanha and Satpura (central India), Pothohar Plateau (Pakistan), dry zone of Sri Lanka, and Similipal (Odisha)
animal.season: Resident; active at night year-round

lore: A suit of armour made from Indian pangolin scales was presented to King George III in 1820 by the Marquess of Hastings and is now displayed at the Royal Armouries in Leeds. Demand for its scales in traditional Chinese medicine, which have no proven medicinal effect, drives most poaching.
funFact: Pangolin scales are made of keratin, the same protein as human fingernails.

summary: The familiar temple and street monkey of northern South Asia and China, with the widest range of any non-human primate. It has shaped modern medicine: the Rh blood factor is named after it, and rhesus monkeys were central to polio vaccine development and early spaceflight.
nativeRange: Afghanistan and Pakistan east through northern India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand and Indochina to China; introduced in Florida and Puerto Rico
abilities: Lives from sea-level mangroves to Himalayan forests above 3,000 m and in big cities
Swims well and readily crosses rivers
Stores food in cheek pouches to eat later in safety

animal.diet: Omnivore: fruits, seeds, leaves, roots, insects and human food
animal.habitat: Forests of many kinds, farmland, temples and towns
animal.lifespan: About 25 years; up to 40 in captivity
animal.size: Body 45–64 cm, tail 20–30 cm; males about 7–12 kg
animal.behaviour: Lives in multi-male, multi-female troops with strict female dominance hierarchies inherited from mothers to daughters.
fieldMarks: Brown-grey monkey with an orange-red rump and lower back
Bare pink to red face and rump
Medium-length tail (shorter than body)
Signs: bold troops around temples, roadsides and picnic spots
animal.lookalikes: Bonnet macaque (south India) has a cap of hair parted in the middle and a longer tail. Assamese macaque is darker and lacks the orange rump. Langurs have black faces and very long tails.
animal.whereToSee: Temples of Vrindavan and Varanasi; Delhi Ridge; Murree and Margalla Hills (Pakistan); Corbett and Kaziranga national parks; Cayo Santiago, Puerto Rico (free-ranging research colony)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Monkeys around Hindu temples are fed as associates of Hanuman, the monkey-god of the Ramayana. India banned the export of rhesus monkeys in 1978 after decades of supplying laboratories worldwide.
funFact: A rhesus monkey named Albert II became the first primate in space in June 1949, aboard a V-2 rocket launched from New Mexico.

summary: One of India's two apes (with the eastern hoolock), a long-armed gibbon of the forests of northeast India, Bangladesh and western Myanmar that swings through the canopy by its arms. Pairs greet each morning with loud duets that carry kilometres through the hills. Its range has shrunk sharply with forest clearance.
nativeRange: Northeast India south of the Brahmaputra, eastern Bangladesh and western Myanmar (west of the Chindwin River)
abilities: Moves by brachiation, swinging arm-over-arm and leaping gaps of several metres
Duets can be heard about 1–2 km away
Disperses seeds of many forest fruit trees

animal.diet: Mainly ripe fruits, especially figs; also leaves, flowers and insects
animal.habitat: Tall evergreen and semi-evergreen forest with a continuous canopy
animal.size: Head and body about 60–90 cm; 6–9 kg; no tail
animal.behaviour: Lives in small family groups of a pair and their young, defending a territory with song. Almost never comes to the ground.
fieldMarks: Silhouette in canopy: tailless ape with very long arms, swinging under branches
Adult males black with conspicuous white eyebrows
Adult females buff to golden-brown with a darker face ringed paler
Signs: loud morning duets, fruit drop under fig trees
animal.voice: Pairs duet in the early morning with escalating whooping calls, often rendered 'hoo-kau, hoo-kau', the female's notes rising into a climax.
animal.lookalikes: Eastern hoolock gibbon (east of the Chindwin, and in Arunachal Pradesh) is very similar; males have separated white brows and females paler. Monkeys such as capped langurs have long tails.
animal.whereToSee: Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary (Assam); Lawachara National Park (Bangladesh); Nokrek and Balpakram (Meghalaya); Dampa Tiger Reserve (Mizoram)
animal.season: Resident; best heard in early mornings, especially in the dry season

lore: Richard Harlan described the species in 1834 from Assam, using a local name for the animal. In Meghalaya, community-protected sacred groves still shelter some hoolock groups.
funFact: Hoolocks have 38 chromosomes, the fewest of any gibbon (others have 44–52), which is one reason they were placed in their own genus, Hoolock, in 2005.

summary: The largest land animal in Asia, a forest elephant that has worked, fought and worshipped alongside people for more than 4,000 years. Fewer than about 50,000 remain in 13 countries, the largest share in India, increasingly squeezed into fragmented forest where conflict with farmers kills both people and elephants.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, southern China, Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: Trunk contains tens of thousands of muscle fascicles and ends in one finger-like tip that can pick up a single fruit
Communicates with low-frequency rumbles partly below human hearing
Opens forest, digs waterholes in dry riverbeds and disperses large seeds
Females lead herds using decades of remembered routes and water sources

animal.diet: Grasses, bark, roots, leaves, bamboo and fruit; also crops such as paddy, sugarcane and banana
animal.habitat: Forest, grassland and scrub with access to water
animal.size: Shoulder height 2–3.2 m; males up to about 5,000 kg
animal.behaviour: Herds of related females and young are led by a matriarch; adult males roam alone or in loose groups and enter musth, a period of high testosterone and aggression marked by fluid from the temple glands.
fieldMarks: Smaller, rounded ears than African elephants; head with twin domes on top
Back level or arched (convex), highest in the middle
Single finger-like projection on the trunk tip
Only some males have tusks; many males (makhnas) and all females have none or tiny tushes
Signs: large round footprints 40–50 cm across, fibrous dung boli, debarked and broken trees
animal.voice: Trumpets when excited or alarmed; also deep rumbles, roars, and high squeaks and chirps.
animal.lookalikes: African savanna and forest elephants have huge ears, a saddle-backed profile and two finger tips on the trunk. Only captive animals could be confused.
animal.whereToSee: Nagarhole–Kabini and Bandipur (Karnataka); Corbett (Uttarakhand); Kaziranga (Assam); Periyar (Kerala); Minneriya and Kaudulla 'Gathering' (Sri Lanka, July–September); Udawalawe (Sri Lanka); Kui Buri (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident; dry-season gatherings near reservoirs and rivers

lore: Ganesha, the elephant-headed Hindu god of beginnings, and Airavata, the white elephant of Indra, make it a sacred animal across India. Elephants appear on Indus Valley seals, and an elephant is carved from the rock above Ashoka's edicts at Dhauli in Odisha.
funFact: In Sri Lanka fewer than one in ten male elephants carries tusks.

summary: The wild ancestor of the domestic water buffalo, a massive bovine of floodplain grasslands with the longest horn span of any living bovid. Fewer than 4,000 are thought to survive, most of them in Assam, and many are at risk of hybridising with domestic buffalo.
nativeRange: Northeast India (Assam, Arunachal), Chhattisgarh, Nepal (Koshi Tappu), Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia
abilities: Spends hot hours submerged in rivers and wallows with only head and horns showing
Horns can span up to about 2 m tip to tip
Herds defend themselves from tigers by charging together

animal.diet: Grasses, sedges, aquatic plants, herbs and crops
animal.habitat: Wet grassland, swamps and river valleys with dense vegetation and water
animal.size: Shoulder height 1.5–1.9 m; 600–1,200 kg
animal.behaviour: Females and calves live in herds of 10–30; bulls form bachelor groups and join herds in the rut, after the monsoon.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: huge, dark grey-black bovine with very wide, crescent-shaped horns swept out and back
Horns flattened and ridged near the base
Pale chevron on the throat and whitish lower legs ('socks')
Sparse coat; signs include mud wallows and trampled reedbed trails
animal.lookalikes: Domestic and feral water buffalo are smaller, with shorter horns and often a sagging belly; hybrids are hard to separate. Gaur has a high shoulder ridge, white socks and shorter upcurved horns.
animal.whereToSee: Kaziranga and Manas national parks, Dibru-Saikhowa (Assam); Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve (Nepal); Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve (Chhattisgarh); Huai Kha Khaeng (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident; best in Kaziranga's dry season (November–April)

lore: The buffalo is the vahana (mount) of Yama, the Hindu god of death, and the demon Mahishasura took buffalo form before Durga slew him. It is the state animal of Chhattisgarh.
funFact: Domestic water buffalo, descended from this species, now number around 200 million worldwide, while their wild ancestor is endangered.

summary: The largest and tallest of all wild cattle, a black-brown forest giant with white stockings and a muscular ridge over its shoulders. India holds the great majority of the world's gaur, and in the Western Ghats herds have learned to graze tea estates and village edges.
nativeRange: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Peninsular Malaysia and southern China
abilities: Adult bulls are so large that even tigers usually avoid them, taking calves instead
Shoulder ridge formed by tall spines on the vertebrae
Climbs steep forested hills up to about 2,800 m

animal.diet: Grasses, bamboo, shoots, leaves, bark and fruit
animal.habitat: Evergreen and deciduous forest with glades and water, usually hilly
animal.size: Shoulder height 1.7–2.2 m; bulls 650–1,500 kg
animal.behaviour: Herds of cows and young are led by an old female; bulls display by standing side-on to show their bulk, a broadside stance.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: huge dark bovine with a high shoulder hump falling to the middle of the back
White or yellowish 'stockings' from hooves to knees
Pale grey-buff boss of hair between the horns; horns curve up and inward
Tracks: large cloven hoofprints about 13 cm long; dung like domestic cattle pats
animal.lookalikes: Banteng (Southeast Asia) has a white rump patch and lacks the strong dorsal ridge. Wild water buffalo has flat, enormous swept-back horns and sparse grey coat. Mithun (domestic Bos frontalis of northeast India) is smaller with straighter horns.
animal.whereToSee: Nagarhole, Bandipur (Karnataka); Kanha and Pench (Madhya Pradesh); Tadoba (Maharashtra); Periyar and Eravikulam (Kerala); Taman Negara (Malaysia); Kui Buri (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident; herds visit forest meadows and salt licks in the dry season

lore: Gaur was the British 'Indian bison' of colonial hunting literature, and is the state animal of Goa and Bihar. Domesticated gaur, the mithun, are a measure of wealth and a sacrificial animal among Naga, Mizo and Adi communities.
funFact: A bull gaur can stand over 2 m at the shoulder, taller than an average man.

summary: The most adaptable big cat, found from the Cape to the Russian Far East and from rainforest to desert and the edges of Mumbai. A stealthy, solitary hunter, it is strong enough to drag prey heavier than itself up into trees. It has lost much of its historic range, and some subspecies, such as the Amur and Arabian leopards, are critically endangered.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, scattered in North Africa and Arabia, Caucasus and Iran, South Asia, Southeast Asia, China and the Russian Far East
abilities: Hoists carcasses of antelope and young giraffe into trees to keep them from lions and hyenas
Eats prey from dung beetles to eland; one of the broadest diets of any cat
Lives in and around large cities such as Mumbai, hunting dogs and pigs at night

animal.diet: Carnivore: antelope, deer, monkeys, wild pigs, rodents, birds, dogs and livestock
animal.habitat: Almost any habitat with cover: forests, savanna, rocky hills, mountains and farmland
animal.size: Males 37–90 kg, females 28–60 kg; 1.6–2.9 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Solitary and mainly nocturnal, stalking to close range before pouncing. Females raise cubs alone, moving them between hidden dens.
fieldMarks: Golden to tawny coat with black rosettes (rings without central spots) on the body, solid spots on head and legs
Long tail, often with white underside of the tip, used as a signal
Compact, low-slung build; relatively large head
Tracks: rounded, about 7–10 cm wide, four toes and no claw marks; signs include kills cached in trees and scratch marks on trunks
animal.voice: A harsh, repeated rasping cough like a saw cutting wood, given to advertise territory.
animal.lookalikes: Cheetah has solid round spots (not rosettes), black 'tear lines' and a slender build. Jaguar (Americas only) is heavier with larger rosettes containing central spots. Snow leopard is grey-white with a very thick tail.
animal.whereToSee: Yala National Park (Sri Lanka); Jhalana Leopard Reserve (Jaipur); Sanjay Gandhi National Park (Mumbai); Bera (Rajasthan); Margalla Hills (Islamabad); Sabi Sands (South Africa); Maasai Mara (Kenya); South Luangwa (Zambia)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Jim Corbett's 'The Man-eating Leopard of Rudraprayag' tells of a leopard that killed over 120 people in Garhwal before he shot it in 1926. The leopard-skin was the regalia of many African kings and chiefs.
funFact: Black panthers are melanistic leopards (or jaguars): in strong light the rosettes still show through the black coat.

summary: The largest cat of the Americas and the only living Panthera there, a powerfully built hunter of rivers and forests. Its bite is so strong for its size that it kills by piercing the skull or crushing turtle shells. The Brazilian Pantanal holds one of the densest jaguar populations anywhere.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina; occasional wanderers into Arizona and New Mexico
abilities: Bite pierces turtle and caiman skulls; it often kills by biting through the back of the skull
Excellent swimmer that hunts caiman and fish in rivers
Top predator whose presence regulates capybara, peccary and caiman populations

animal.diet: Carnivore: capybara, peccaries, deer, caiman, turtles, armadillos, fish and livestock
animal.habitat: Dense forest, swamps and seasonally flooded wetlands, generally near water
animal.size: 56–96 kg typically; Pantanal males can exceed 120 kg; 1.6–2.7 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Solitary, mostly crepuscular, and hunts both by stalking on land and by ambush from riverbanks.
fieldMarks: Large, deep-chested cat with a broad head and short, thick legs
Rosettes large and angular, often enclosing one or more black spots
Tail relatively short compared with a leopard's
Tracks: broad, round pugmarks 9–12 cm along riverbanks; signs include tree scratching and scrapes
animal.voice: A deep, hoarse series of grunts, often likened to sawing wood; also called 'roncar' in Brazil.
animal.lookalikes: Leopard (Old World only) is lighter-built with smaller rosettes without central spots. Ocelot is much smaller with chain-like stripes. Puma is plain tawny.
animal.whereToSee: Porto Jofre and the Cuiabá, Piquiri and Three Brothers rivers (northern Pantanal, Brazil); Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary (Belize); Iwokrama (Guyana); Calakmul (Mexico); Corcovado (Costa Rica)
animal.season: Resident; Pantanal river sightings peak in the dry season, roughly July–October

lore: The Olmec carved were-jaguar figures over 3,000 years ago, and Maya kings took jaguar names such as Yaxuun Bahlam (Bird Jaguar). Aztec elite warriors were the 'jaguar knights' (ocelomeh).
funFact: Belize's Cockscomb Basin, made a no-hunting forest reserve in 1984 and a wildlife sanctuary in 1986, is widely credited as the world's first protected area set aside for jaguars.

summary: A large, plain-coated cat with the widest range of any wild land mammal in the Americas, from the Yukon to the Strait of Magellan. It cannot roar, but purrs, chirps and screams. Pumas kill deer and guanaco and leave scraps that feed scavengers from condors to beetles.
nativeRange: Western Canada and the western USA (plus Florida), Mexico, Central America and all of South America to Patagonia
abilities: Leaps up to about 5 m vertically and much farther horizontally
Kills prey several times its size with a bite to the neck
Young males disperse hundreds of kilometres; one travelled about 2,900 km from the Black Hills of South Dakota to Connecticut

animal.diet: Carnivore: deer, elk, guanaco, peccary, rodents and hares
animal.habitat: Any terrain with cover and prey, from sea level to 5,800 m in the Andes
animal.size: Males 53–100 kg, females 29–64 kg; 1.5–2.75 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Solitary and territorial. Caches kills under leaves and earth and returns to feed over several days.
fieldMarks: Plain tawny-grey to reddish coat, pale underneath
Small rounded head; long, heavy tail with a dark tip
Dark marks on the sides of the muzzle; kittens are spotted
Tracks: round, 7–10 cm, three-lobed heel pad, no claw marks; signs include kills covered with litter and scrapes under trees
animal.voice: Does not roar; gives whistles, chirps, purrs and, in breeding season, piercing screams.
animal.lookalikes: Jaguar is spotted and stockier. Jaguarundi is much smaller with a weasel-like body. Bobcat and lynx have short bobbed tails.
animal.whereToSee: Torres del Paine National Park (Chile, the best place to watch them); Patagonia Park (Chile); Big Bend and the Rocky Mountains (USA, rarely seen); Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge
animal.season: Resident; Torres del Paine tracking tours run most of the year, best in autumn and winter (April–September)

lore: Tradition holds that the Inca city of Cusco was laid out in the shape of a puma, with Sacsayhuamán as its head.
funFact: The puma holds a Guinness World Record for the animal with the most names: over 40 in English alone.

summary: The largest lynx and Europe's third-largest predator, a long-legged, tuft-eared cat of forest and mountain from Scandinavia to the Tibetan Plateau. Reintroductions have returned it to Switzerland, Germany and France, and the pale Himalayan form lives in Ladakh and northern Pakistan.
nativeRange: Northern and central Europe, Russia, Central Asia, the Caucasus, Ladakh, Gilgit-Baltistan, Tibet and northeastern China
abilities: Kills deer such as roe deer and even reindeer, prey several times its weight
Large, fur-padded paws act as snowshoes
Ear tufts and facial ruff help in visual communication

animal.diet: Roe deer, chamois, musk deer, reindeer, hares, marmots and birds
animal.habitat: Dense forest and rocky mountain terrain; in Ladakh, arid rocky slopes and willow scrub
animal.size: 18–30 kg (males larger); body 80–130 cm, short tail 11–25 cm
animal.behaviour: Solitary hunter that ambushes from cover or stalks; returns to large kills for several nights.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: long legs, short body and short bob tail with a black tip
Black ear tufts and a broad facial ruff
Coat greyish to reddish with varying dark spots; Himalayan lynx pale sandy and faintly spotted
Tracks: round, 7–9 cm, no claw marks; in snow very wide due to hairy feet; signs include roe-deer kills covered with snow or leaves
animal.voice: Mostly silent; in the late-winter breeding season gives far-carrying, mournful calls and hisses.
animal.lookalikes: Iberian lynx (Spain and Portugal only) is smaller with bold dark spots. Caracal (Pakistan and India lowlands) is plain tawny with very long ear tufts and no ruff or bob tail. Wildcat has a long, ringed tail.
animal.whereToSee: Bohemian Forest (Czechia–Germany); Swiss Jura and Alps; Carpathians (Slovakia, Romania); Białowieża (Poland); Hemis and Changthang (Ladakh); Finnish taiga hides
animal.season: Resident; winter snow makes tracking easiest (January–March is breeding season)

lore: Greek legend linked the lynx to Lynceus, the Argonaut who could see through walls, and the 'lynx-eyed' ideal named Rome's Accademia dei Lincei (founded 1603). Theophrastus described 'lyngurium', a gem supposedly formed from hardened lynx urine.
funFact: The Accademia dei Lincei, named after the lynx's keen sight, counted Galileo among its early members.

summary: A bear-like giant weasel of the far north, famous for its endurance and strength. Wolverines travel tens of kilometres a day over mountains, crunch frozen carcasses with powerful jaws and store food in snow and rock crevices.
nativeRange: Circumpolar: Scandinavia, northern Russia, Siberia, Alaska, Canada and the high Rockies and Cascades of the northwestern USA
abilities: Crushes frozen meat and bone with a strong jaw and a molar turned sideways in the upper jaw
Covers huge home ranges, over 1,000 km² for some males
Climbed some 1,500 m up Mount Cleveland, Glacier National Park, in about 90 minutes in winter (a radio-collared male)

animal.diet: Scavenged carcasses of reindeer, moose and other ungulates; also hunts hares, rodents, birds and sometimes reindeer in deep snow
animal.habitat: Remote tundra, taiga and alpine areas with deep spring snow cover for dens
animal.size: Males 11–18 kg, females 7–12 kg; body 65–105 cm
animal.behaviour: Solitary and wide-ranging. Females dig dens in deep snow to give birth in late winter.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: small bear-like body, arched back, short legs and bushy tail
Dark brown coat with a pale buff band along each flank from shoulders to tail
Pale mask across the forehead
Tracks: five-toed, about 10–13 cm, often in a bounding '2–1–2' or '3–4' pattern in snow
animal.lookalikes: Bear cubs lack the pale side-stripe and have smaller tails; badgers are greyer with a striped face; fishers and martens are slimmer and smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Kuhmo and Lieksa wildlife hides, eastern Finland; Norwegian and Swedish mountains (e.g. Dovrefjell); Denali (Alaska); Kluane (Yukon)
animal.season: Resident; hides in Finland give sightings April–September

lore: Olaus Magnus, in his 1555 History of the Northern Peoples, claimed the 'gulo' gorged until it had to squeeze between two trees to empty its belly. Its Latin name means 'glutton'.
funFact: Wolverine fur resists frost, so Inuit and other northern peoples trimmed parka hoods with it.

summary: A small fox of the high Arctic with the warmest fur of any mammal, turning white in winter and brown-grey in summer (or bluish-grey year-round in the 'blue' morph). Arctic foxes follow polar bears to scavenge, cache lemmings and seabird eggs, and some cross sea ice for thousands of kilometres.
nativeRange: Circumpolar tundra of Eurasia and North America, Greenland, Iceland, Svalbard and the Commander and Pribilof Islands
abilities: Does not begin to shiver until the temperature falls to about −70 °C
A young female walked 3,500 km from Svalbard to Ellesmere Island, Canada, in 76 days across sea ice (2018)
Can have litters of up to about 20 pups in good lemming years

animal.diet: Lemmings and voles, seabirds and eggs, fish, carrion including polar-bear kill leftovers, berries
animal.habitat: Tundra, mountain plateaus, sea-ice margins and coastal cliffs
animal.size: Body 46–68 cm, tail 25–42 cm; 2.5–9 kg
animal.behaviour: Dens are dug in sandy mounds and some are reused for centuries. Pairs raise pups together.
fieldMarks: Small, compact fox with short legs, short rounded ears and a short muzzle
Winter: pure white (white morph) or slate blue-grey (blue morph); summer: brownish-grey with paler belly
Very bushy tail and furred soles
Signs: dens on mounds with many entrances and lush green vegetation, fertilised by prey remains
animal.lookalikes: Red fox, increasingly moving north, is larger, redder, with larger pointed ears and longer legs. In white, distant snowshoe hare or ptarmigan may be mistaken briefly.
animal.whereToSee: Hornstrandir Nature Reserve (Iceland); Svalbard; Dovrefjell–Sunndalsfjella (Norway); Churchill (Manitoba); Commander Islands (Russia)
animal.season: Resident; white coat October–May

lore: The Arctic fox was Iceland's only native land mammal when the Norse arrived around 870 CE. In Finnish folklore, the aurora is 'revontulet', 'fox fires', said to be sparks from a fox's tail brushing the snow.
funFact: Its species name lagopus means 'hare-foot', for the dense fur that covers the soles of its feet.

summary: The largest living deer, a long-legged browser of northern forests and lakes. Bulls grow broad, palmate antlers that can span more than 1.5 m and are shed each winter. Moose wade and even dive in lakes to feed on water plants rich in sodium.
nativeRange: Boreal and mixed forests of northern Europe, Russia and Siberia, Mongolia, northeastern China, Canada, Alaska and the northern USA
abilities: Dives to about 5–6 m and stays under for nearly a minute to graze aquatic plants
Can close its nostrils underwater
Long legs let it wade through deep snow and step over fallen trees
Grows a new set of antlers, up to about 30 kg, every spring and summer

animal.diet: Browse: willow, birch, aspen shoots and bark; aquatic plants in summer
animal.habitat: Northern forest with lakes, bogs, rivers and young regrowth
animal.size: Shoulder height 1.4–2.1 m; bulls 380–700 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary. In the autumn rut bulls spar and call, and cows with calves are fiercely protective.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: very tall humped shoulders, long legs, short neck and a long, overhanging muzzle
Dewlap ('bell') of skin hanging from the throat
Bulls' antlers broad and palm-shaped (palmate), less often branching
Tracks: cloven hoofprints 13–15 cm long; signs include stripped bark, browsed tops of young trees and large piles of oval pellets
animal.voice: Cows give a long, nasal, moaning call in the rut; bulls answer with deep grunts or croaks.
animal.lookalikes: Wapiti/elk (Cervus canadensis) is reddish with a pale rump patch and branched (not palmate) antlers. Reindeer are smaller, with white necks and antlers in both sexes.
animal.whereToSee: Algonquin Provincial Park (Ontario); Denali (Alaska); Grand Teton (Wyoming); Baxter State Park (Maine); Biebrza National Park (Poland); forests of central Sweden and Norway
animal.season: Resident; rut in September–October; summer sightings in lakes and ponds at dawn and dusk

lore: Paintings and carvings of moose (elk) appear in Stone Age rock art across Scandinavia and Russia, including the Alta rock carvings in Norway. Julius Caesar's Gallic War records a tale that 'alces' had no knee joints and slept leaning against trees.
funFact: The word 'moose' comes from an Eastern Algonquian name, often glossed as 'twig-eater' or 'he strips off bark'.

summary: The only deer in which both sexes grow antlers, adapted to Arctic tundra and boreal forest. Wild caribou herds make some of the longest overland migrations on Earth, while domestic reindeer have been central to Sámi, Nenets and Evenki life for centuries. Many wild herds have declined steeply, and the species is listed as Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Circumpolar: Scandinavia, Russia, Siberia, Greenland, Alaska and Canada; introduced to South Georgia (since removed) and Kerguelen
abilities: Some herds travel over 1,000 km a year between winter range and calving grounds
Eyes see ultraviolet light, helping them spot lichen and predators against snow
Its tapetum changes from gold in summer to deep blue in winter, improving vision in the long dark
Digs through snow ('cratering') with broad hooves to reach lichens

animal.diet: Lichens ('reindeer moss', Cladonia) in winter; grasses, sedges, willow leaves and mushrooms in summer
animal.habitat: Arctic tundra, mountain plateaus and northern taiga
animal.size: Shoulder height 0.8–1.5 m; 80–180 kg (males larger)
animal.behaviour: Gathers in vast herds on migration and at calving grounds, where most calves are born within a few weeks in late May–June. Calves can follow their mothers within hours of birth.
fieldMarks: Both sexes carry long, sweeping antlers with a forward-projecting 'shovel' brow tine
Greyish-brown body with pale neck and white rump and tail
Large, broad, concave hooves
Signs: lichen grazing craters in snow, trails worn through tundra; tracks crescent-shaped and almost round
animal.lookalikes: Moose is far larger with a long overhanging muzzle and palmate antlers only on bulls. Musk ox is shaggy with horns, not antlers.
animal.whereToSee: Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and Denali (Alaska); Hardangervidda and Snøhetta (Norway, wild reindeer); Finnish and Swedish Lapland (herded reindeer); Western Greenland around Kangerlussuaq
animal.season: Resident or migratory: spring migration April–June; autumn rut September–October

lore: Reindeer herding has defined Sámi culture for centuries, and Nenets herders of the Yamal peninsula still migrate with their herds over 1,000 km a year. A single reindeer first pulled Santa's sleigh in the 1821 poem 'Old Santeclaus with Much Delight'; 'A Visit from St. Nicholas' (1823, attributed to Clement Clarke Moore) raised the team to eight and named them.
funFact: A tendon slipping over a bone in the foot makes walking reindeer give off a clicking sound that helps herds stay together.

summary: An Ice Age survivor of the high Arctic, a shaggy, short-legged bovid more closely related to goats than to cattle. Its underwool, qiviut, is among the warmest natural fibres. Facing wolves, herds form a tight circle with calves in the middle and horns outward.
nativeRange: Arctic Canada and Greenland; reintroduced or introduced to Alaska, Norway (Dovrefjell), Sweden, Siberia (Taymyr, Wrangel Island)
abilities: Qiviut underwool is warmer than sheep's wool by weight and is shed each spring
Defensive ring formation repels wolves, though not human hunters
Survives winters of −40 °C on frozen sedges and willows dug from snow

animal.diet: Grasses, sedges, Arctic willow, herbs and lichens
animal.habitat: Arctic tundra and river valleys with thin snow cover
animal.size: Shoulder height 1.1–1.5 m; bulls 270–410 kg
animal.behaviour: Bulls charge each other head-on in the late-summer rut, colliding with a crash audible far away. Herds of 10–30 are typical.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: low, boxy dark-brown animal with long skirt of guard hair reaching near the ground
Horns with a massive central 'boss' across the forehead, curving down then up beside the face
Pale saddle and pale lower legs
Signs: tufts of shed qiviut on willows and rocks in early summer; rounded hoofprints
animal.lookalikes: Bison (not in Arctic) has a tall hump and short upturned horns. Reindeer are slimmer with antlers. Takin (Himalaya) is golden with differently curved horns.
animal.whereToSee: Dovrefjell–Sunndalsfjella National Park (Norway); Kangerlussuaq (Greenland); Nunivak Island and Nome (Alaska); Banks Island, Aulavik National Park (Canada); Wrangel Island (Russia)
animal.season: Resident year-round; summer is best for access

lore: Musk oxen were hunted out of Alaska by the early 1900s; a few dozen animals brought from Greenland and released on Nunivak Island in 1935–36 founded most of today's Alaskan herds. Inuit traditionally used the horns for ladles, bows and fish spears.
funFact: Despite its name, the musk ox is not an ox: it is a goat-antelope, closer to sheep and goats than to cattle, and its nearest living relatives appear to be the gorals of Asia's mountains.

summary: An acrobatic baleen whale with enormous wing-like flippers, known for breaching, bubble-net feeding and some of the most complex songs in the animal kingdom. After commercial whaling ended, most populations have recovered strongly. It migrates thousands of kilometres between cold feeding grounds and tropical breeding grounds every year.
nativeRange: All oceans, from polar feeding grounds to tropical breeding grounds; a non-migratory population lives in the Arabian Sea
abilities: Groups blow spiralling 'bubble nets' to herd fish into a tight ball, then lunge through it
Males sing complex, structured songs that change over seasons and spread between populations across ocean basins
Migrations of up to about 8,000 km one way, among the longest of any mammal
Flippers up to a third of body length, with knobbly leading edges that improve lift

animal.diet: Krill and small schooling fish such as herring, capelin, anchovies and sand lance
animal.habitat: Coastal and continental-shelf waters; tropical shallows for breeding
animal.size: 12–16 m; 25–30 tonnes (females larger)
animal.behaviour: Breaches, slaps flippers and tails, and travels in loose groups. Mothers and calves stay together for about a year.
fieldMarks: Very long white or partly white flippers
Small, stubby dorsal fin on a hump, two-thirds of the way back
Knobbly tubercles on the head and jaw
Raises the tail flukes high before a deep dive; black-and-white underside pattern of each fluke is unique
Bushy blow, 3–4 m tall
animal.voice: Males' songs are long sequences of moans, groans, whoops and squeals arranged in repeated themes, lasting up to half an hour and repeated for hours.
animal.lookalikes: Gray whale lacks a dorsal fin and long flippers and is mottled grey. Fin and minke whales have tall, sickle-shaped dorsal fins and seldom raise their flukes. Right whales lack a dorsal fin and have white callosities.
animal.whereToSee: Hervey Bay (Queensland); Maui (Hawaii); Vava'u (Tonga); Silver Bank (Dominican Republic); Stellwagen Bank (Massachusetts); Monterey Bay (California); Juneau (Alaska); Húsavík (Iceland); Gulf of Masirah and the Dhofar coast (Oman) for Arabian Sea whales
animal.season: Northern breeding grounds January–April; northern feeding grounds May–October; Australia and Tonga July–October

lore: Roger Payne and Scott McVay's 1971 paper and the album 'Songs of the Humpback Whale' (1970) helped spark the 'Save the Whales' movement; a recording flew on the Voyager Golden Records in 1977.
funFact: Its genus name Megaptera means 'big-winged', for flippers that can reach 5 m long.

summary: A mottled, barnacle-encrusted baleen whale that feeds on the seafloor by sucking up mud and straining out tiny crustaceans. Eastern Pacific gray whales migrate some 15,000–20,000 km a year between the Arctic and the lagoons of Baja California, where mothers famously approach small boats. The Atlantic population was hunted to extinction by the 18th century.
nativeRange: North Pacific: eastern population from the Bering and Chukchi seas to Baja California; a small western population off Sakhalin and Kamchatka
abilities: Rolls on its side and sucks sediment from the seafloor, filtering amphipods through short baleen
Leaves feeding pits on the seabed that recycle sediments and nutrients
A tagged western gray whale, 'Varvara', swam about 22,500 km from Sakhalin to Mexico and back in 2011–12, the longest mammal migration then recorded

animal.diet: Benthic amphipods, ghost shrimp, crab larvae and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters; warm lagoons for calving
animal.size: 13–15 m; up to about 35 tonnes
animal.behaviour: Travels close to shore on migration. In Baja lagoons some mothers bring calves to be touched by people in small boats.
fieldMarks: Mottled grey skin covered with white-orange barnacle and whale-lice patches
No dorsal fin: a low hump followed by a series of 'knuckles' along the tail stock
Heart-shaped or V-shaped blow, 3–4 m high
Narrow, slightly arched head; flukes often lifted on deep dives, with a notch and pale scarring
animal.lookalikes: Humpback has a dorsal fin and very long white flippers. Bowhead and right whales are black with no barnacle mottling (right whales have callosities).
animal.whereToSee: Laguna San Ignacio, Ojo de Liebre (Scammon's) Lagoon and Magdalena Bay (Baja California, Mexico); Monterey Bay and Point Reyes (California); Depoe Bay (Oregon); Tofino (British Columbia)
animal.season: Baja lagoons January–April; migration along California December–May; some 'resident' whales stay off Oregon and British Columbia in summer

lore: Whalers called mothers 'devil fish' for their violent defence of calves in Scammon's lagoon in the 1850s. The Makah of Washington State have a treaty right to hunt gray whales, central to their culture.
funFact: A gray whale seen off Israel and Spain in 2010 was the first in the Atlantic basin for centuries, likely having crossed the ice-reduced Arctic.

summary: The only baleen whale that lives in the Arctic year-round, a black giant with a massive bow-shaped skull that can smash through sea ice to breathe. Bowheads are the longest-lived mammals known: harpoon points from the 1800s found in living whales, and eye-lens dating, indicate ages of over 200 years.
nativeRange: Arctic and sub-Arctic seas: Bering–Chukchi–Beaufort, Baffin Bay, Hudson Bay, East Greenland–Svalbard–Barents, Sea of Okhotsk
abilities: Can break through sea ice at least 60 cm thick with its head
Longest-lived mammal: one individual was estimated at about 211 years old
Longest baleen of any whale, up to about 4 m
Thickest blubber of any animal, up to about 50 cm

animal.diet: Copepods, krill and other small zooplankton, skimmed at the surface or near the bottom
animal.habitat: Ice-edge waters, leads and polynyas of the Arctic
animal.lifespan: Often over 100 years; 200+ in some individuals
animal.behaviour: Migrates along leads in the sea ice in spring and back south in autumn. Male bowheads sing diverse, ever-changing songs in winter: nearly 200 distinct song types were recorded off Svalbard over three years.
fieldMarks: Huge, black body with no dorsal fin
Strongly arched, bow-shaped mouthline; head up to a third of body length
White chin patch, often with black spots; pale band near the tail
V-shaped blow from two widely spaced blowholes; two humps (head and back) visible when surfacing
animal.voice: Highly varied songs of whoops, moans and trills, likened to jazz because new songs appear each year.
animal.lookalikes: North Atlantic and North Pacific right whales lack the white chin and have rough white callosities on the head. Gray whale is mottled with barnacles.
animal.whereToSee: Disko Bay (West Greenland, spring); Isabella Bay/Igaliqtuuq (Baffin Island, late summer); Utqiaġvik, Alaska (spring migration); Shantar Islands (Sea of Okhotsk); Svalbard (rare)
animal.season: Spring migration April–June; late-summer feeding in Baffin and Beaufort seas; wintering in the Bering Sea

lore: For Iñupiat whaling communities of northern Alaska, the spring bowhead hunt and the Nalukataq festival that follows are the heart of the year. Basque, Dutch and British whalers hunted 'Greenland whales' at Svalbard from the early 1600s.
funFact: In 2007 a fragment of a harpoon made in New Bedford in the 1880s was found embedded in a bowhead caught off Alaska.

summary: A pure-white Arctic whale with a bulbous, shape-changing forehead, so talkative that sailors called it the 'sea canary'. Thousands gather each summer in warm river estuaries to calve, feed and moult their skin against the gravel. Some even travel far up rivers.
nativeRange: Arctic and sub-Arctic waters: Hudson Bay, Baffin Bay, Beaufort and Bering seas, White Sea, Svalbard, Sea of Okhotsk; isolated populations in the St Lawrence estuary and Cook Inlet
abilities: Unfused neck vertebrae let it nod and turn its head, unusual among whales
Changes the shape of its fatty melon to focus echolocation and perhaps to signal
Navigates and finds breathing holes in dense pack ice using echolocation
Has entered rivers far inland, e.g. hundreds of kilometres up the Yukon, Amur and Rhine

animal.diet: Fish (cod, salmon, capelin), squid, shrimp, crabs and worms
animal.habitat: Coastal Arctic waters, estuaries and ice edges
animal.lifespan: Typically 35–50 years; some estimated to reach 80
animal.size: 3–5.5 m; up to about 1,600 kg (males larger)
animal.behaviour: Social, travelling in pods that can merge into gatherings of thousands in estuaries. Calves are born grey and whiten over several years.
fieldMarks: All-white adult (grey young) with no dorsal fin — only a low ridge along the back
Rounded, mobile melon and short beak
Broad, paddle-shaped flippers that curl at the tips in older males
Small, low blow; often seen in shallow, muddy estuary water
animal.voice: A wide repertoire of whistles, chirps, squeals, clicks and bell-like trills audible through boat hulls, giving the name 'sea canary'.
animal.lookalikes: Narwhal is mottled grey-black, and males carry a spiral tusk. In poor light, a white wave crest or ice floe can be mistaken for a beluga's back.
animal.whereToSee: Churchill River estuary, Manitoba (Hudson Bay, tens of thousands in July–August); Saguenay–St. Lawrence Marine Park, Tadoussac (Quebec); Cunningham Inlet, Somerset Island (Nunavut); Solovetsky Islands, White Sea (Russia); Turnagain Arm, Alaska
animal.season: Estuary gatherings late June–August; winter at the pack-ice edge

lore: Inuit communities hunt belugas for muktuk (skin and blubber), a key source of vitamin C in the traditional Arctic diet. In the 1980s a US Navy beluga named NOC was recorded imitating human speech patterns.
funFact: Belugas moult each summer, rubbing off old yellowed skin on estuary gravel to reveal fresh white skin beneath.

summary: A slow, gentle aquatic grazer of warm coasts and rivers from Florida to Brazil, related more closely to elephants than to seals. Manatees cannot tolerate cold water, so Florida's population crowds into warm springs and power-plant outflows each winter. Boat strikes and seagrass loss are its main threats.
nativeRange: Southeastern USA (Florida, occasionally north to Virginia and the Gulf coast), Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, Central America and northeastern South America to Brazil
abilities: Molars are replaced continuously from the back, moving forward like a conveyor belt as worn teeth fall out
Eats about 10% of its body weight in plants each day
Moves freely between fresh and salt water
Prehensile split upper lip grasps vegetation

animal.diet: Seagrasses, freshwater plants, algae and mangrove leaves
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, rivers, estuaries and springs warmer than about 20 °C
animal.size: 2.7–3.5 m; 400–550 kg (exceptionally 1,500 kg)
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary or in mother–calf pairs, but aggregates in warm-water refuges. Surfaces every few minutes to breathe, more often when active.
fieldMarks: Large, grey-brown, wrinkled body, often scarred by boat propellers and coated with algae
Broad, rounded, paddle-shaped tail
Flippers with three or four fingernails
Signs: 'footprints' (smooth circles of water) on the surface as the tail pushes down, and a nose-only breath
animal.lookalikes: Dugong (Indo-Pacific only) has a whale-like fluked tail. Amazonian manatee (fresh water only) lacks nails and usually has a white chest patch. West African manatee is very similar but lives only off West Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Crystal River and Three Sisters Springs, Blue Spring State Park and Manatee Lagoon (Florida); Swallow Caye (Belize); Puerto Rico; Laguna de Términos (Mexico)
animal.season: Florida springs November–March (cold fronts bring the biggest gatherings); year-round in the Caribbean

lore: In January 1493 Columbus recorded seeing three 'sirens' off Hispaniola that were 'not as pretty as they are painted'. Taíno peoples carved manatee bone into ritual objects such as vomiting spatulas.
funFact: A manatee's lungs lie along its back and help it control buoyancy, letting it hang motionless in the water.

summary: The only strictly marine herbivorous mammal, a seagrass grazer of warm Indo-Pacific shallows with a whale-like fluked tail. Dugongs plough seagrass meadows like underwater cows, leaving feeding trails across the seabed. Australia holds most of the world's population; in India they survive in tiny numbers in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Gulf of Kutch and Andaman Islands.
nativeRange: Coastal Indo-West Pacific from East Africa and the Red Sea through the Arabian Gulf, South and Southeast Asia to northern Australia, New Guinea and Vanuatu
abilities: Uproots whole seagrass plants, leaving feeding trails that can promote regrowth of fast-growing, more nutritious seagrasses
Can live over 70 years
Mature males and some old females grow short tusks

animal.diet: Seagrasses, especially roots and rhizomes; occasionally invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow, sheltered, warm coastal waters with seagrass
animal.behaviour: Feeds by rooting through the sediment with its muscular, downturned snout. Mothers nurse a single calf for about 18 months.
fieldMarks: Grey to brown, smooth fusiform body
Whale-like fluked tail with a median notch (not a rounded paddle)
Broad, downturned snout with a bristly upper lip disc
Signs: meandering, sandy 'feeding trails' through seagrass beds; surfaces showing only nostrils
animal.lookalikes: Manatees (Atlantic only) have rounded paddle tails. Sea turtles also graze seagrass but have shells and heads that stay up longer.
animal.whereToSee: Shark Bay and Moreton Bay (Australia); Marsa Alam and Marsa Abu Dabbab (Red Sea, Egypt); Marawah Marine Reserve (Abu Dhabi); Coron, Palawan (Philippines); Bazaruto Archipelago (Mozambique); Palk Bay Dugong Conservation Reserve (Tamil Nadu, India)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Dugongs and manatees, the order Sirenia, are named for the sirens of Greek myth, and seafarers' tales of mermaids are often traced to them. In 2022 Tamil Nadu declared India's first Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay.
funFact: The dugong's closest living relatives on land are elephants.

summary: A gigantic, tusked pinniped of the Arctic, gathering in haul-outs of thousands on ice floes and beaches. Walruses find clams by touch with hundreds of sensitive whiskers and suck them out of their shells. Loss of summer sea ice now forces enormous crowds onto shore, where stampedes kill calves.
nativeRange: Arctic seas: Pacific walrus in the Bering and Chukchi seas; Atlantic walrus from Canadian Arctic and Greenland to Svalbard and the Kara Sea
abilities: Uses tusks up to about 1 m long as ice picks to haul out — 'Odobenus' means 'tooth-walker'
Hundreds of stiff, sensitive whiskers detect clams in seafloor mud
Produces powerful suction that pulls clam bodies from their shells, and jets water to dig them out
Can slow its heart rate on dives; most feeding dives last under 10 minutes, though dives of about 25 minutes have been recorded

animal.diet: Mainly bivalve molluscs; also worms, snails, crabs; occasionally seals
animal.habitat: Shallow continental-shelf waters with sea ice; land haul-outs when ice is absent
animal.size: Males 2.7–3.6 m and up to about 1,500 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Extremely gregarious, lying in dense heaps. Males sing underwater courtship songs of knocks, taps and bell-like tones for days in winter.
fieldMarks: Huge, wrinkled cinnamon-brown to pinkish body (pinker when warm)
Two long ivory tusks in both sexes (longer in males)
Broad, bristly 'moustache' of whiskers
No external ears; hind flippers can turn forward to walk on land
Signs: haul-out beaches with flattened gravel, shells and tusk-gouged ice
animal.voice: Loud roars, grunts and barks on haul-outs; underwater, males produce knocks, clicks and a ringing bell-like sound.
animal.lookalikes: Bearded seal has long whiskers but no tusks and is far smaller. Elephant seals (not Arctic) have a trunk-like nose and no tusks.
animal.whereToSee: Round Island, Walrus Islands State Game Sanctuary (Alaska); Svalbard (Poolepynten, Torellneset); Point Lay, Alaska; Cape Serdtse-Kamen and Wrangel Island (Chukotka); Igloolik and Foxe Basin (Nunavut)
animal.season: Svalbard and Round Island haul-outs June–September

lore: The 12th-century Lewis chessmen, found in Scotland, were carved mainly from walrus ivory, likely traded from Norway and Greenland. Norse Greenlanders paid tithes and trade in walrus tusks.
funFact: Walruses can sleep while floating vertically, inflating air sacs in their necks like built-in life jackets.

summary: The apex predator among Antarctic seals, a sleek, reptilian-headed hunter famous for ambushing penguins at the ice edge. It also sieves huge quantities of krill through intricately lobed cheek teeth. It is the only seal that regularly hunts other warm-blooded animals.
nativeRange: Antarctic and sub-Antarctic waters, especially the pack ice; vagrants reach South America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Huge gape and long canines for seizing penguins and young seals
Interlocking three-pointed cheek teeth strain krill from water like a sieve
Patrols penguin colonies and catches birds as they enter or leave the water

animal.diet: Krill, penguins, fish, squid and other seals (especially crabeater pups)
animal.habitat: Edge of the Antarctic pack ice and sub-Antarctic islands
animal.size: 2.5–3.5 m; up to about 600 kg; females larger than males
animal.behaviour: Solitary. During the breeding season (November–January) males hang upside-down underwater and sing loud trills and moans.
fieldMarks: Long, slender, serpentine body with a large, reptile-like head
Dark grey back and pale, black-spotted underside and throat
Wide mouth that appears to 'smile'
Long fore-flippers used for swimming; often seen lounging alone on ice floes
