animal.voice: Underwater, males produce loud, long trills and low moans during the breeding season, audible to hydrophones far away.
animal.lookalikes: Weddell seal is chubbier with a small rounded head and short muzzle. Crabeater seal is paler, smaller-headed and usually in groups. Southern elephant seal is massive and shorter-flippered.
animal.whereToSee: Antarctic Peninsula: Pléneau Island, Paradise Bay, Cuverville Island and Brown Bluff penguin colonies; South Georgia; occasionally New Zealand coasts in winter
animal.season: Antarctic cruise season November–March; highest at penguin colonies when chicks fledge (January–February)

lore: On Shackleton's Endurance expedition in 1916 a leopard seal chased Thomas Orde-Lees across the sea ice until Frank Wild shot it. In 2003 a leopard seal drowned British marine biologist Kirsty Brown while she was snorkelling at Rothera Station.
funFact: Photographer Paul Nicklen described a female leopard seal repeatedly bringing him penguins, as if teaching him to hunt.

summary: The world's largest rodent, a semi-aquatic grazer of South American wetlands that lives in social groups and seldom strays far from water. With partly webbed feet and eyes, ears and nostrils set high on its head, it can lie almost submerged. Birds, monkeys and other animals often perch on or lounge beside it.
nativeRange: South America east of the Andes, from Colombia and Venezuela to northeastern Argentina and Uruguay; also Panama
abilities: Can stay submerged for about five minutes and sleep in the water with only its nose exposed
Re-ingests its own soft droppings to extract more nutrients from grass
Teeth grow continuously to cope with abrasive grasses

animal.diet: Grasses, aquatic plants, bark and fruit; selective grazer
animal.habitat: Marshes, rivers, lakes and flooded grasslands with nearby dry ground
animal.behaviour: Lives in groups of 10–20 led by a dominant male; groups merge into hundreds in the dry season around remaining water.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: barrel-shaped, tailless, blunt-headed rodent the size of a large dog
Coarse, sparse reddish-brown to grey hair
Dominant males have a large, bare scent gland ('morrillo') on the top of the snout
Tracks: four toes on front feet, three on hind, partly webbed; signs include grazing lawns and droppings near water
animal.voice: Barks sharply in alarm; also whistles, clicks, purrs and grunts within the group.
animal.lookalikes: Lowland paca is smaller with white spotted rows on its flanks. Coypu (nutria) is much smaller with a long rat-like tail and orange incisors.
animal.whereToSee: Esteros del Iberá (Argentina); Pantanal (Brazil); Los Llanos, e.g. Hato El Cedral (Venezuela); Lago Paranoá and city parks in Brasília and Curitiba (Brazil)
animal.season: Resident year-round; dry-season gatherings around shrinking water bodies (roughly July–October in the Pantanal)

lore: Venezuelan Catholics traditionally eat salted capybara (chigüire) during Lent, a custom said to rest on a colonial-era church ruling that the semi-aquatic animal counted as fish. Its name comes from Tupi ka'apiûara, usually translated 'grass-eater'.
funFact: The Brazilian city of Curitiba and the wealthy Nordelta suburb of Buenos Aires both have well-known urban capybara populations.

summary: A toothless insect-eater with a tubular snout, a tongue about 60 cm long and a huge, flag-like tail. It raids termite mounds and ant nests for just a minute or so each, flicking its tongue up to 150 times a minute, and moves on before the colony's soldiers mount a defence. Fire, roads and habitat loss have made it Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Central America (rare, Honduras southward) and South America east of the Andes to northern Argentina; extinct in Uruguay and much of Central America
abilities: Eats around 30,000 ants and termites a day
Forelimb claws up to 10 cm tear open concrete-hard termite mounds and can disable a jaguar in defence
Has one of the lowest body temperatures of any land mammal, about 33 °C
Walks on its knuckles to protect its long claws

animal.diet: Ants and termites; occasionally beetle larvae and fruit
animal.habitat: Open grassland, savanna, wetlands and forest edges
animal.lifespan: About 15 years in the wild; over 30 in captivity
animal.size: Body about 1–1.2 m plus a 65–90 cm tail; 27–50 kg
animal.behaviour: Solitary. Mothers carry the single young on their back for months, its dark stripe lining up with hers as camouflage.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: long tubular head, low body and enormous bushy tail held level or over the body like a blanket
Bold black diagonal stripe edged with white running from throat over the shoulder
Pale front legs with a black band above huge curved claws
Signs: termite mounds with fresh, fist-sized holes torn in the side; knuckle-walking tracks turned inward
animal.lookalikes: Southern and northern tamanduas are much smaller, climb trees and have a short, naked prehensile tail. No other animal in its range has the long snout and huge tail together.
animal.whereToSee: Serra da Canastra and Emas national parks (Brazilian cerrado); Pantanal (Brazil); Esteros del Iberá (Argentina, reintroduced); Los Llanos (Venezuela, Colombia)
animal.season: Resident; often active in daylight in cool weather, nocturnal in hot weather

lore: In Guaraní the animal is yurumí, and the giant anteater appears in Indigenous stories across the Gran Chaco and cerrado. Since 2007 a rewilding programme in Argentina has reintroduced giant anteaters to the Iberá wetlands, where they had disappeared.
funFact: The anteater's tongue is anchored to its sternum, not its mouth, allowing it to extend so far.

summary: A bony-shelled digger of the Americas that has spread steadily north through the USA since the 19th century. Females almost always give birth to genetically identical quadruplets, all from one fertilised egg. It is also one of the few animals other than humans that naturally carries leprosy.
nativeRange: South America (to northern Argentina), Central America, Mexico and the southern and central USA (expanding north)
abilities: Gives birth to identical quadruplets from a single egg (polyembryony)
Can hold its breath for about six minutes, walking across stream bottoms or gulping air to float
Leaps about 1 m into the air when startled
Digs dozens of burrows used later by other animals

animal.diet: Insects and other invertebrates (beetles, ants, termites, larvae), small vertebrates, eggs and fruit
animal.habitat: Forest, scrub and grassland with soft soil
animal.size: Body 38–58 cm, tail 26–45 cm; 3–7 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal in summer and active by day in cool weather. Digs for food with its nose to the ground, sniffing out prey.
fieldMarks: Leathery, armoured shell with a shoulder shield, a hip shield and 7–11 (usually 8–9) movable bands in between
Long, armoured, tapering tail
Small, pointed head and large upright ears
Signs: shallow conical feeding holes 'snout-pokes' in lawns and leaf litter; burrows about 20 cm wide
animal.lookalikes: Other Dasypus species in South America are very similar; seven-banded and southern long-nosed armadillos differ in band count and range. Six-banded armadillo is yellowish with fewer, wider bands.
animal.whereToSee: Florida and Texas, e.g. Aransas National Wildlife Refuge and Big Thicket; Pantanal (Brazil); Los Llanos (Venezuela)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Aztecs called it ayotochtli, 'turtle-rabbit', and Andean musicians made the charango, a small lute, from armadillo shells. It is the state small mammal of Texas.
funFact: Its startle leap is so high that it often strikes the undersides of cars, a major cause of roadkill.

summary: The largest living primate, found in two subspecies: Grauer's gorilla of the lowland forests of eastern DR Congo, and the famous mountain gorilla of the Virunga volcanoes and Bwindi. Mountain gorillas, studied since Dian Fossey's work in the 1960s, have increased to just over 1,000 and were downlisted from Critically Endangered to Endangered in 2018, while the species as a whole remains Critically Endangered because Grauer's gorillas have declined sharply.
nativeRange: Virunga Mountains (Rwanda, Uganda, DR Congo), Bwindi Impenetrable Forest (Uganda) and eastern DR Congo lowland and montane forests
abilities: Silverback males can weigh over 200 kg and are several times stronger than people
Builds a fresh nest of leaves and branches to sleep in every night
Disperses seeds and opens gaps in forest through feeding and movement

animal.diet: Mainly leaves, stems, shoots and pith (wild celery, nettles, bamboo shoots); fruit when available; occasional ants
animal.habitat: Montane and bamboo forest (mountain gorillas, up to about 4,000 m) and lowland rainforest (Grauer's)
animal.size: Males 1.5–1.8 m standing, 140–220 kg; females about half as heavy
animal.behaviour: Lives in groups led by one or more silverbacks. Males display by standing upright and beating their chests with cupped hands, a sound carrying over 1 km.
fieldMarks: Very large black ape; mountain gorillas have long, thick, black hair
Adult males with a silver saddle on the back
Massive head with a prominent sagittal crest in males; broad nostrils
Signs: night nests on the ground with dung, trails of trampled vegetation and broken celery stems; knuckle prints
animal.voice: Chest-beating 'pok-pok' drumming, hoots, roars and soft, contented 'belch' grumbles between group members.
animal.lookalikes: Western gorillas (Gorilla gorilla) of West and Central Africa are browner-grey, with a reddish crown and shorter hair. Chimpanzees are much smaller, with large ears and long arms.
animal.whereToSee: Volcanoes National Park (Rwanda); Bwindi Impenetrable and Mgahinga Gorilla national parks (Uganda); Virunga National Park (DR Congo); Kahuzi-Biega National Park (DR Congo, Grauer's gorilla)
animal.season: Resident; trekking runs year-round, drier months June–September and December–February are easiest

lore: Dian Fossey founded the Karisoke Research Center in Rwanda in 1967 and wrote 'Gorillas in the Mist' (1983) before her murder in 1985. Rwanda's annual Kwita Izina ceremony names each newborn mountain gorilla.
funFact: The species is named for German officer Robert von Beringe, who shot two on Mount Sabyinyo in 1902, the first known to science.

summary: One of humans' two closest living relatives, found only south of the Congo River in DR Congo. Unlike chimpanzees, bonobo societies are led by alliances of females, and they defuse tension with sexual and social contact rather than violence. They will even share food with strangers.
nativeRange: Lowland rainforests of the Congo Basin south of the Congo River, DR Congo only
abilities: Shares DNA with humans at roughly the same level (about 98.7%) as chimpanzees
Shows empathy, consolation and sharing with unfamiliar individuals in experiments
Captive bonobo Kanzi learned to communicate with hundreds of lexigram symbols

animal.diet: Fruit, leaves, pith, seeds, insects and occasionally small mammals
animal.habitat: Humid lowland forest and mosaic forest–savanna south of the Congo River
animal.size: 70–83 cm sitting; males about 39 kg, females about 31 kg
animal.behaviour: Lives in fission–fusion communities of 30–80. Females form strong bonds and collectively dominate males.
fieldMarks: Slender ape with long legs and a relatively small, round head
Black face from birth and pink lips
Long black hair parted neatly in the middle on the crown
Signs: night nests high in trees; high-pitched calls distinguish them from chimpanzee pant-hoots
animal.voice: Higher-pitched hoots and whistles than chimpanzees, including a sharp, bird-like 'hi-hi' call.
animal.lookalikes: Chimpanzee (north of the Congo River) is more robust, with a paler face in youth, larger ears and no central hair parting. Ranges do not overlap.
animal.whereToSee: Lola ya Bonobo Sanctuary (near Kinshasa); Wamba and the Luo Scientific Reserve; LuiKotale and Salonga National Park; Lomako-Yokokala Faunal Reserve (all DR Congo)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The bonobo was recognised as a distinct species only in 1929, from a skull in a Belgian museum. In the Wamba region, a Mongandu taboo against eating bonobos, who are seen as ancestral kin, helped protect them.
funFact: Bonobos were not recognised as a species until 1929, more than 150 years after chimpanzees, because they look so similar.

summary: Madagascar's most familiar lemur, a sun-loving primate of dry forests and rocky canyons in the island's south and southwest. Troops are led by females, and males fight 'stink fights' by wiping their tails with scent and waving them at rivals. Although common in zoos, wild numbers have fallen steeply with forest loss and the pet trade.
nativeRange: Southern and southwestern Madagascar
abilities: Sunbathes in a 'yoga' posture, belly and arms open to the morning sun
Males hold 'stink fights', anointing their tails with scent from wrist and chest glands
Spends more time on the ground than any other lemur

animal.diet: Fruit (especially tamarind), leaves, flowers, bark, sap and insects
animal.habitat: Gallery forest along rivers, dry scrub, spiny forest and rocky outcrops
animal.size: Body about 40 cm, tail 55–62 cm; 2.2 kg
animal.behaviour: Lives in troops of up to about 30 with female dominance. Troop members huddle in 'lemur balls' to keep warm on cold nights.
fieldMarks: Long black-and-white ringed tail (about 13 alternating black and white bands) held up like a flag when walking
Grey back and paler underside
White face with black eye-patches and a dark nose
Signs: troops on the ground and rocks; scent marks on saplings
animal.voice: Cat-like mews to keep contact, loud yelps and wails as alarm calls, and a purring 'contented' call.
animal.lookalikes: No other lemur has a ringed tail. Brown and red-fronted lemurs are browner with plain tails.
animal.whereToSee: Anja Community Reserve; Isalo National Park; Berenty Private Reserve; Andringitra National Park; Tsimanampesotse National Park (all Madagascar)
animal.season: Resident; births in September–October, so young are seen clinging to mothers in spring

lore: Many Malagasy communities hold fady (taboos) against harming lemurs, and in Anja the community-run reserve has turned the species into a source of tourism income. Linnaeus described it in 1758 as the type of the genus Lemur, after the Roman spirits of the dead (lemures).
funFact: Surveys published in 2016–2017 counted only about 2,000–2,400 ring-tailed lemurs at the sites studied, raising fears the wild population had crashed; the true total is debated because many sites remain unsurveyed.

summary: A tiny, pencil-limbed nocturnal primate of Sri Lanka's wet southwest, with enormous forward-facing eyes for hunting insects at night. It moves slowly and silently along branches, then lunges with both hands. The related grey slender loris lives in drier Sri Lanka and southern India.
nativeRange: Endemic to the wet zone of southwestern Sri Lanka, including a highland form in the central hills
abilities: Huge eyes with a reflective tapetum for vision in near darkness
Grasp so strong it can hang for long periods, aided by special blood vessels (retia mirabilia) in its limbs
Eats toxic or bad-tasting insects that other predators avoid

animal.diet: Mostly insects (including ants and beetles), plus other invertebrates, small lizards, eggs and some plant matter
animal.habitat: Wet lowland and submontane forest and nearby gardens with dense vine tangles
animal.size: Body about 17–26 cm, no external tail; 85–170 g
animal.behaviour: Strictly nocturnal and arboreal. Sleeps by day curled up in a ball among dense foliage, often in small groups.
fieldMarks: Very thin limbs and tiny body with no tail
Huge round eyes ringed with dark patches and divided by a white stripe down the nose
Reddish-brown fur (redder than the grey slender loris)
At night, eyes show bright orange-red eyeshine in torchlight; moves hand over hand slowly
animal.lookalikes: Grey slender loris (Loris lydekkerianus) of Sri Lanka's dry zone and southern India is greyer with a paler underside. Slow lorises (northeast India and Southeast Asia) are much stockier.
animal.whereToSee: Masmullah Proposed Forest Reserve; Kottawa Forest and Kanneliya Forest Reserve; Sinharaja Forest Reserve (all Sri Lanka); best with a guided night walk
animal.season: Resident; active at night year-round

lore: In Sri Lankan and South Indian folk belief, loris eyes and body parts were used in charms and remedies, which, with the pet trade, has long contributed to their persecution.
funFact: Its species name tardigradus means 'slow-stepping', the same root as the microscopic tardigrades.

summary: The largest surviving carnivorous marsupial, a stocky, black scavenger with a bone-crushing bite and a spine-tingling screech. Since the 1990s a transmissible cancer, devil facial tumour disease, has killed the majority of wild devils, spread directly by bites. Insurance populations on Maria Island and in mainland sanctuaries now help safeguard the species.
nativeRange: Tasmania; extinct on the Australian mainland for about 3,000 years (small reintroduced populations in New South Wales sanctuaries since 2020)
abilities: Among the strongest bites for its size of any living mammal, crushing bone and eating almost every part of a carcass
Clears carcasses and suppresses feral cats, helping protect small native mammals
Travels up to about 16 km a night foraging

animal.diet: Mainly carrion (wallabies, possums, wombats, livestock); also hunts small animals
animal.habitat: Forest, woodland, coastal heath and farmland across Tasmania
animal.size: Body 52–80 cm, tail 23–30 cm; 6–12 kg (males larger)
animal.behaviour: Solitary but gathers noisily at carcasses, sorting out feeding order with screams, growls and gaping displays. Young spend about 100 days in the pouch.
fieldMarks: Stocky, dog-sized black marsupial with a large head and short legs
White band across the chest and often white patches on the rump
Ears flush pink-red when the animal is stressed
Tracks: five-toed front, four-toed hind; signs include large scats full of bone and fur fragments on tracks
animal.voice: Unearthly screeches, growls and high-pitched screams, especially at shared carcasses at night.
animal.lookalikes: Spotted-tailed quoll is smaller, slimmer and covered in white spots. Feral cats have pointed ears and long tails.
animal.whereToSee: Cradle Mountain–Lake St Clair National Park and Narawntapu National Park (Tasmania); Maria Island (insurance population); Bonorong and Devils@Cradle sanctuaries; Aussie Ark, Barrington Tops (NSW)
animal.season: Resident; breeding in March; juveniles disperse in late summer

lore: Early European settlers in Tasmania named it the 'devil' after its unearthly nocturnal screams. With the extinction of the thylacine in 1936, it became the world's largest surviving carnivorous marsupial.
funFact: Devil facial tumour disease is one of very few known contagious cancers: the tumour cells themselves are transmitted between animals.

summary: A sturdy, burrowing marsupial of southeastern Australia and Tasmania, famous for its cube-shaped droppings. Its backward-facing pouch keeps soil out while digging, and its burrows give shelter to many other animals, notably during bushfires.
nativeRange: Southeastern Australia (New South Wales, Victoria, southeastern South Australia and Queensland border), Tasmania and Flinders Island
abilities: Produces cube-shaped scats, shaped by varying elasticity of the intestinal wall
Backward-facing pouch prevents soil entering when digging
Digs burrow systems up to about 20 m long
Tough cartilage plate on the rump blocks burrow entrances against predators

animal.diet: Grasses, sedges, roots and tubers
animal.habitat: Forest, woodland, heath and grassland with suitable digging soil
animal.size: About 1 m long; 20–35 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; grazes slowly, but can sprint at about 40 km/h. Leaves scats on rocks and logs as territorial markers.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: low, barrel-shaped, almost tailless animal with a broad head
Coarse fur, grey-brown to sandy or black
Large, hairless, granular nose; short rounded ears
Signs: cube-shaped scats placed on rocks, logs and track edges; large burrow entrances with spoil heaps
animal.lookalikes: Southern hairy-nosed wombat has a furry nose, longer pointed ears and silkier fur, and lives in drier South Australia. Echidnas are spiny.
animal.whereToSee: Maria Island and Cradle Mountain (Tasmania); Wilsons Promontory (Victoria); Bendeela Recreation Area, Kangaroo Valley (New South Wales); Kosciuszko National Park
animal.season: Resident; often active by day in cool winter weather

lore: The word 'wombat' comes from the Dharug language of the Sydney area. The Pre-Raphaelite poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti kept a pet wombat in London in 1869.
funFact: A wombat can produce around 80–100 cube-shaped scats a night.

summary: One of only five living monotremes, the egg-laying mammals. A spine-covered ant- and termite-eater with a sticky tongue, it is found across almost all of Australia and in New Guinea. Females lay a single leathery egg into a temporary pouch and suckle the hatchling from milk patches, without nipples.
nativeRange: Australia (all states including Tasmania and Kangaroo Island) and lowland southern New Guinea
abilities: Lays eggs; the young ('puggle') hatches in the pouch after about 10 days
Snout carries electroreceptors that may detect insects in moist soil
Digs straight down into soil within minutes to escape predators, leaving only spines exposed
Enters torpor and hibernation, dropping its body temperature to a few degrees above the surroundings

animal.diet: Ants, termites, beetle larvae and earthworms
animal.habitat: Almost every terrestrial habitat in Australia, from snowfields to deserts
animal.lifespan: Up to about 45 years in the wild
animal.behaviour: Solitary. In winter, 'echidna trains' form, with up to 10 or more males following a female nose-to-tail for days.
fieldMarks: Round, spine-covered body with cream, black-tipped spines among brown fur
Slim, tube-like hairless snout (beak)
Short legs with powerful digging claws; hind feet point backwards
Signs: snout-sized holes in soil, torn open termite mounds and ant nests, scats full of ant remains and soil; tracks show backward-pointing hind claws
animal.lookalikes: No other Australian mammal has spines. Introduced hedgehogs do not occur in Australia. Long-beaked echidnas (New Guinea highlands) are larger with longer, downcurved snouts.
animal.whereToSee: Kangaroo Island (South Australia); Tasmania, e.g. Freycinet and Cradle Mountain; Wilsons Promontory (Victoria); Royal National Park (New South Wales); widespread in bushland
animal.season: Resident; most active on mild days in spring; echidna trains June–September

lore: An echidna appears on the Australian five-cent coin. In many Aboriginal traditions stories explain how the echidna got its spines, often through a fight or punishment involving spears.
funFact: When first described in 1792 it was thought to be a type of anteater; its egg-laying was confirmed only in 1884.

summary: The only mammals that feed exclusively on blood, vampire bats make a tiny cut in sleeping livestock or wild mammals and lap the flowing blood. Heat-sensing pits on the nose guide them to blood vessels near the skin, and their saliva contains anticoagulants studied for stroke drugs. Roostmates famously share regurgitated blood with those who failed to feed.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to northern Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; Trinidad and Margarita islands
abilities: Senses infrared heat with nose pits, using a specially modified TRPV1 receptor
Saliva anticoagulant (draculin and plasminogen activators) keeps blood flowing; a derivative, desmoteplase, was trialled as a stroke drug
Runs and leaps on the ground on its forelimbs, unusual for a bat
Shares blood with hungry roostmates, preferring those who shared with them before

animal.diet: Blood of mammals, mainly cattle, horses and pigs; also wild mammals
animal.habitat: Caves, hollow trees, mines and buildings within reach of mammal prey
animal.lifespan: Up to about 29 years in captivity; about 9 in the wild
animal.size: Body 7–9 cm, wingspan about 35–40 cm; 25–40 g
animal.behaviour: Leaves the roost after full darkness, often avoiding bright moonlight. Drinks about half its own body weight in blood in a 20–30 minute feed.
fieldMarks: Short, flat, pug-like snout with a small U-shaped nose-leaf
Long, strong thumbs used for walking
No tail; grey-brown fur
Sharp, blade-like upper incisors; signs include small cuts and blood trickles on livestock, and roosts that smell of ammonia with dark, tarry droppings
animal.lookalikes: White-winged and hairy-legged vampire bats (Diaemus, Diphylla) feed mainly on birds and have white wing-tips or furry legs. Fruit-eating leaf-nosed bats have tall spear-shaped nose leaves.
animal.whereToSee: Lamanai Archaeological Reserve (Belize, night bat tours); caves of Mexico's Yucatán; Pantanal and Amazon cattle ranches (Brazil)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: European naturalists named it after the vampire of Slavic folklore; in turn, Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897) gave the bat a central place in vampire fiction. Rabies spread by vampire bats is a major veterinary problem across Latin America.
funFact: A vampire bat that misses two nights of blood meals can starve, which is why sharing among roostmates matters so much.

summary: A small woodland bat with ears almost as long as its body, which it uses to hear the rustling of insects on leaves. It 'whispers' its echolocation calls and often picks moths and spiders off foliage, hovering in the canopy. It commonly roosts in the roof spaces of old houses, barns and churches.
nativeRange: Europe from Ireland and Iberia to the Urals, the Caucasus and western Siberia
abilities: Ears about three-quarters the length of its head and body
Very quiet, low-intensity echolocation, plus passive listening to prey sounds
Gleans prey off leaves and can hover
Hibernates in caves, cellars and trees, sometimes with ears tucked under the wings

animal.diet: Moths, beetles, earwigs, spiders and other arthropods
animal.habitat: Woodland, wooded gardens and parks; roosts in attics, barns, churches and tree holes
animal.size: Body 4–5 cm, wingspan 23–28 cm; 6–12 g
animal.behaviour: Often carries large moths to a favourite perch to eat, leaving discarded wings in piles beneath.
fieldMarks: Enormous ears joined at the base over the forehead
At rest, ears folded back under the wings, leaving the long pointed tragus showing
Fluffy brown fur, pale below; pinkish-brown face
Signs: piles of moth and butterfly wings under porches or barn rafters (feeding perches); droppings in attics
animal.lookalikes: Grey long-eared bat (Plecotus austriacus) is greyer, with a darker face and longer tragus; reliable separation often needs measurements. Other bats have much shorter ears.
animal.whereToSee: Old churches, barns and country houses in Britain and Ireland; woodlands across Scandinavia and central Europe; Bat Conservation Trust and similar guided bat walks
animal.season: Active roughly April–October; hibernates November–March

lore: Long-eared bats in church roofs are a classic part of English rural life; in the UK all bat species and roosts are protected by law. In medieval Europe bats were linked with witchcraft and the night.
funFact: It can hear a ladybird walking on a leaf, using sound alone to find prey.

summary: A wetland mole whose nose is ringed by 22 pink, fleshy tentacles, the most sensitive touch organ known in any mammal. It touches its surroundings about 10 times a second and can identify and eat a prey item in a fraction of a second. It also swims and forages underwater.
nativeRange: Eastern Canada and northeastern USA, south along the Appalachians to Georgia; also coastal Carolinas
abilities: Its star carries about 25,000 touch receptors (Eimer's organs) served by over 100,000 nerve fibres
Identifies and eats prey in as little as about 120 milliseconds, among the fastest foragers known
Smells underwater by blowing out air bubbles and re-inhaling them
Swims well and tunnels into stream banks and under ice

animal.diet: Aquatic insects, worms, small crustaceans, molluscs and small fish
animal.habitat: Poorly drained wet soils of marshes, bogs, wet meadows and stream banks
animal.size: Body 10–13 cm, tail 6–8 cm; 35–75 g
animal.behaviour: Active day and night year-round, foraging in tunnels, on the surface and underwater, even under winter ice.
fieldMarks: Unmistakable ring of 22 pink fleshy rays around the nostrils
Dark, dense, water-repellent fur
Long hairy tail (thickens in winter as fat is stored)
Broad digging forefeet; signs include molehills in wet soil and tunnels leading into water
animal.lookalikes: Eastern and hairy-tailed moles lack the star and live in drier soils; shrews are smaller with pointed snouts.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen; wet meadows and bog edges in Nova Scotia and Quebec; Great Smoky Mountains National Park; Adirondacks (New York); often found by cats or in pitfall surveys
animal.season: Resident; active year-round

lore: It was described by Linnaeus in 1758 as Sorex cristatus; neuroscientist Kenneth Catania's studies since the 1990s made the star a model for how brains map touch.
funFact: Despite its appearance, the star is not used to grab food; it is purely a touch organ, while the mole's teeth do the eating.

summary: The largest slow loris and one of the world's few venomous primates. When threatened it raises its arms over its head, licks a gland on the inner elbow, and mixes the secretion with saliva to deliver a painful, sometimes dangerous bite. It is the only slow loris in India and is heavily hunted for the pet and traditional-medicine trades.
nativeRange: Northeast India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, southern China, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam
abilities: Brachial (elbow) gland secretion combined with saliva makes a toxic bite that can cause severe swelling and anaphylactic shock in people
Its grip can hold for hours, aided by networks of blood vessels in the limbs
Feeds on tree gum by gouging bark with its tooth-comb, an important dry-season food

animal.diet: Plant gum and sap, nectar, fruit, insects, snails, birds' eggs
animal.habitat: Evergreen and semi-evergreen forest and bamboo groves with continuous canopy
animal.size: Body 26–38 cm; 1–2.1 kg; tail vestigial
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal and slow-moving, but capable of quick lunges. Sleeps curled in a ball in dense foliage by day.
fieldMarks: Stocky, woolly primate with a round head and almost no tail
Dark brown stripe along the spine reaching the crown
Large eyes encircled by dark rings with a white stripe between
Bright orange eyeshine in torchlight at night; slow, deliberate climbing
animal.lookalikes: Pygmy slow loris (Indochina) is much smaller and redder. Slender lorises are thin-limbed and live only in southern India and Sri Lanka.
animal.whereToSee: Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary (Assam); Lawachara National Park (Bangladesh); Dampa Tiger Reserve (Mizoram); Khao Yai National Park (Thailand); night walks with guides
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In Bengali it is called the 'shy monkey' (lajjabati banor) because it covers its face with its hands when caught in light. Its body parts have been sold in markets in Southeast Asia and China for traditional remedies.
funFact: Slow lorises are the only primates confirmed to produce venom.

summary: A nocturnal, shrew-like insectivore of Hispaniola that injects venom through grooves in its lower incisors, one of very few venomous mammals. Its lineage split from other insectivores around 70–78 million years ago, before the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs, making it a living link to the Cretaceous mammal fauna.
nativeRange: Hispaniola (Dominican Republic and Haiti)
abilities: Delivers toxic saliva through a deep groove in each second lower incisor ('solenodon' means 'grooved tooth')
Lineage survived the end-Cretaceous mass extinction
Long, flexible snout supported by a ball-and-socket joint probes crevices

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, millipedes, worms, small vertebrates and some fruit
animal.habitat: Forest and scrub with limestone crevices, caves and hollow logs for shelter
animal.lifespan: Several years; up to about 11 in captivity
animal.size: Body 28–33 cm, tail 17–26 cm; 0.6–1 kg
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal. Females have teats far back near the hips, and young may be dragged along clinging to them.
fieldMarks: Large, rat-sized shrew-like animal with a very long, naked, flexible snout
Small eyes and coarse brown fur with reddish sides of the head
Long, naked, scaly tail
Signs: conical 'nose-pokes' in leaf litter and soil where it has probed for invertebrates
animal.lookalikes: Cuban solenodon (Atopogale cubana) lives only in eastern Cuba. Introduced rats and mongooses lack the long probing snout and odd, waddling gait.
animal.whereToSee: Very hard to see; nocturnal surveys in Sierra de Bahoruco and Jaragua national parks, Los Haitises and Pedernales (Dominican Republic); Massif de la Hotte (Haiti)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Hispaniolan solenodon was described by Johann Friedrich Brandt in 1833 from a specimen sent from Haiti, and was so unusual it was named 'paradoxus'. Long listed as Endangered, it was downlisted to Least Concern by the IUCN in 2020 as surveys showed it to be more widespread than feared.
funFact: Introduced dogs, cats and small Indian mongooses are its main predators: the solenodon evolved without fast-moving carnivores.
